senses.definition: A length of some object.
senses.example: a segment of rope

senses.definition: One of the parts into which any body naturally separates or is divided; a part divided or cut off; a section; a portion.
senses.example: a segment of an orange; a segment of a compound or divided leaf

senses.definition: A portion.
senses.example: The third segment of the highway was closed for repairs.

senses.definition: A straight path between two points that is the shortest distance between them; a line segment.
senses.example: The segment connecting points A and B is shorter than any other path.

senses.definition: The part of a circle between its circumference and a chord (usually other than the diameter).
senses.example: The shaded segment lies between the arc and the chord of the circle.

senses.definition: The part of a sphere cut off by a plane.
senses.example: The volume of the spherical segment depends on the height of the cut.

senses.definition: Any of the pieces that constitute an order tree.
senses.example: In the parse, each segment of the ordered tree holds one subtree.

senses.definition: A discrete unit of speech: a consonant or a vowel.
senses.example: The vowel in the word cat is a segment that linguists transcribe as /æ/.

senses.definition: A part of a broadcast program, devoted to a topic.
senses.example: The news showed a segment on global warming.

senses.definition: A region of memory or a fragment of an executable file designated to contain a particular part of a program.
senses.example: The loader placed the code segment at a fixed address in memory.

senses.definition: A portion of an itinerary: it may be a flight or train between two cities, or a car or hotel booked in a particular city.
senses.example: Our trip had three segments: a flight to Denver, a rental car, and a hotel.

senses.definition: A portion of an organ whose cells are derived from a single cell within the primordium from which the organ developed.
senses.example: Each segment of the kidney develops from a single progenitor cell in the primordium.

senses.definition: One of several parts of an organism, with similar structure, arranged in a chain; such as a vertebra, or a third of an insect's thorax.
senses.example: Each segment of the earthworm's body looks much like the one before it.

senses.definition: To divide into segments or sections.
senses.example: Segment the essay by topic.

core.definition: A distinct part of a larger whole, such as a group of customers who share similar traits in a dataset.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable in the noun; the verb shifts stress to the second syllable: seg-MENT. The second syllable is a reduced 'muhnt', so do not pronounce both vowels fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'segment' in business, marketing, statistics and data science to mean a group defined by shared traits. In everyday speech it usually refers to a part of an orange or a section of a TV show. Its verb form means to divide something into parts.

distinctions.note: 'Section' is a general word for a part; 'segment' often implies a part identified by a defining principle or division.
A 'cluster' is found by an algorithm based on similarity; a 'segment' may be defined in advance by business rules.

examples.everyday: I just saw a segment about the new bridge on the local news.
examples.professional: We need to segment our customers by purchase frequency before we target the campaign.
examples.analytical: A segment is only meaningful if its boundaries rest on a principled criterion rather than convenient labels.

nuance.analogy: Like slices of an orange: each piece is part of the fruit, separated by clear lines.
nuance.etymology: From Latin segmentum, 'a piece cut off', from secare, 'to cut'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable in the noun, which makes it sound like the verb.
Using 'segment' as a synonym for 'segment of time' without a clear sense of division.

segment.etymology: From Latin *segmentum* (“a piece cut off, a strip, segment of the earth, a strip of tinsel”), from *secāre* (“to cut”).

senses.definition: A person who is skilled at, professes, or practices seismology.
senses.example: The seismologist explained that the small tremors were normal for this fault line.

core.definition: A scientist who studies earthquakes, seismic waves and the Earth's vibrations, often to assess hazards.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAH, the o is pronounced 'ah', and the final -ist is short, like 'jist'. Do not stress the first syllable as in SAIZ-muh-list.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a respected professional title.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use seismologist for scientists who work at the U.S. Geological Survey, universities and engineering firms. It is a formal job title, not slang. In casual talk people often say earthquake expert, but seismologist is the word you would see in a news story or on a résumé.

distinctions.note: A geophysicist studies many physical properties of the Earth; a seismologist specializes in earthquakes and seismic waves.
A geologist studies rocks, minerals and Earth history; a seismologist focuses on how the ground vibrates.

collocations: a seismologist at the U.S. Geological Survey

examples.everyday: My cousin is a seismologist, so she always hears about the small tremors before they make the news.
examples.professional: The seismologist on our team reviewed the sensor data and recommended a second inspection of the foundation.
examples.analytical: A seismologist's forecast depends on models of how stress builds along faults, and those models are always uncertain.

nuance.analogy: A seismologist is like a doctor for the ground, listening to its tremors and reading the signs of strain beneath the surface.
nuance.etymology: From seismology plus the agent suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in SAIZ-muh-list.
Confusing seismologist, a person, with seismic, which is an adjective and describes things.

senses.definition: A form of attention (machine learning method) where input sequence is compared with itself, i.e. the keys and queries are the same.
senses.example: The transformer model uses self-attention so each token can weigh every other token in the sentence.

senses.definition: Conscious attention to one's own physiological and emotional state and behavior.
senses.example: Her therapist encouraged daily self-attention, noticing her moods and reactions before they escalated.

core.definition: A machine learning mechanism where each element of an input sequence weighs its relationship to every other element in the same sequence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEN, with a light secondary stress on self. The -tion ending sounds like 'shun' and is unstressed, so avoid saying 'self-ah-TEN-shun' with a strong middle vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American data science and AI, self-attention is a standard technical term, especially in transformer models. Engineers say it in papers, code reviews and meetings. In psychology, the term has a different meaning, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Attention is the general mechanism; self-attention is the case where queries, keys and values all come from the same input.
Cross-attention draws from two different sequences, while self-attention uses only one.

examples.everyday: My coworker explained that the model uses something called self-attention, but I'm still confused.
examples.professional: We replaced the recurrent layer with a self-attention layer, which reduced training time significantly.
examples.analytical: Self-attention allows each token to aggregate information from the entire sequence, which is why transformers handle long-range dependencies well.

nuance.analogy: Self-attention is like a group discussion where every person looks at everyone else's comments before deciding what to say.
nuance.etymology: Self from Old English self, 'same'; attention from Latin attendere, 'to stretch toward'.
common_mistakes: Confusing the machine learning sense with the psychology sense of self-attention.
Thinking self-attention is only about the model paying attention to itself, rather than to the other positions in the same sequence.

conversation.text: In self-attention, the queries, keys, and values all come from the same sequence.
Self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, which is why long documents get expensive fast.
In this example, the self-attention weights show the pronoun attending strongly to the noun it refers to.

senses.definition: Having self-similarity; having parts that resemble the whole, as a fractal has.

core.definition: Having parts that look like smaller copies of the whole, as a fractal does.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SIM, with self carrying lighter secondary stress. The final -ar is a weak schwa followed by a clear American r, so say SIM-uh-ler, not SIM-uh-lar.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise descriptive term with no emotional charge, though mathematicians admire the elegance of such patterns.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in mathematics, physics, computing and writing about fractals, coastlines, ferns or branching trees. In casual talk it sounds overly technical, and people more often say the pattern repeats at every scale. Use the term when precision matters, such as in a paper or a technical presentation.

distinctions.note: A fractal is an object or set that is typically self-similar; self-similar names the property, while fractal names the object.
Similar means alike in some respects, while self-similar means each part is alike the whole at smaller scales within the same object.

examples.everyday: Have you seen Romanesco broccoli? Each little floret looks like a tiny copy of the whole head, which is kind of self-similar.
examples.professional: The network traffic we're modeling looks self-similar across time scales, so the burstiness at one-second intervals also shows up at one-minute intervals.
examples.analytical: A coastline is self-similar only within limits, since real shorelines repeat their irregularity over a finite range of scales rather than infinitely.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of Russian nesting dolls, where each doll is a scaled-down version of the largest.
nuance.etymology: From self- plus similar, from Latin similis, like.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable (sim-ih-LAR) instead of SIM.
Using it in everyday talk to mean similar to yourself; outside technical contexts it usually sounds confusing.

senses.definition: A member of a modern people that speak a Semitic language.
A member of any of a number of peoples of ancient southwestern Asia and East Africa such as the Akkadians, Assyrians, Arameans, Phoenicians, Canaanites, Hebrews, Arabs, or Aksumites.
senses.example: Historians of the ancient Near East study Akkadians and Phoenicians as early Semites.

senses.definition: A descendant of any of these peoples.
senses.example: Her family, as Semites from the region, preserved an ancient language through many generations.

senses.definition: A descendant of the biblical Patriarch Shem.
senses.example: According to Genesis, the Semites descended from Shem, one of Noah's three sons.

senses.definition: A Jew.
senses.example: Historians note that the term Semite was often used as a slur for Jews in the 1930s.

senses.definition: Synonym of Semitic.
senses.example: The seminar compared Semite languages such as Hebrew and Arabic with Indo-European grammar.

core.definition: A member of a people who speak or historically spoke a Semitic language, such as Arabs, Hebrews, or Akkadians.

pronunciation.tip: The input IPA has a syllable dot that is not needed. Stress the first syllable and say the final part as ite, rhyming with bite. Avoid saying it as suh-MITE.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarly use, but the word is sensitive because it is tied to the term antisemitism. Use it carefully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Semite mainly in history, linguistics, and religious studies. It is a broad label for people of the ancient and modern Near East who speak related languages, so it can be confusing if used as a simple synonym for Jewish or Arab. In everyday speech people name the specific group instead.

distinctions.note: Semite is the noun for a person or people, while Semitic is the adjective for the languages or cultures.
Jewish refers to a religion or ethnic community, and it is narrower than Semite, which covers several peoples.

examples.everyday: My history class covered the ancient Semites who lived in Mesopotamia and the Levant.
examples.professional: The museum's curator wrote the exhibit label about the Semites who lived in the city of Ugarit.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the category Semite ever described a single shared culture or only a family of related languages.

nuance.analogy: Like the word European, which names a broad region and many distinct nations inside it.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 1780s from Shem, the name of Noah's son in Genesis.
common_mistakes: Using Semite as a simple synonym for Jewish, which is inaccurate and can cause misunderstanding.
Confusing the noun Semite with the adjective Semitic in a sentence.
nuance.biblical_note: Shem means name in Hebrew, and the term comes from him. Genesis 9:26 has Noah bless the LORD as the God of Shem, Genesis 10:21-31 lists Shem's descendants in the Table of Nations, and Genesis 11:10-26 traces his line down to Abram.

semite.etymology: From *Sem*, *Shem* *ite*, from Late Latin *Sēm*, from Ancient Greek *Σήμ*, from Biblical Hebrew *שם*.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see send,‎ up.
senses.example: Fears of war sent oil prices up by 10%.

senses.definition: To imitate (someone or something) for the purpose of satirical humor.
senses.example: The program accurately sends up the British Civil Service system at Whitehall.

senses.definition: To put in prison.
senses.example: The judge sent him up for three years.

senses.definition: To cause (something, e.g. sparks) to erupt.
senses.example: Where the metal touched the asphalt, it sent up a shower of sparks.

core.definition: To make fun of someone or something by imitating them in an exaggerated, comic way, often on TV or in a parody.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on UP, with a short ʌ vowel, not 'oop'. SEND has a weaker secondary stress, so say it clearly but lighter.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative, since it means mocking someone. It can be affectionate when the parody is friendly and clever.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use send up for TV shows, comedians, and movies that imitate famous people or institutions, such as 'That sketch really sends up the news anchors.' It can also mean to put someone in prison, but this sense is dated slang. In a serious discussion, avoid send up because it can sound dismissive; say 'criticize' or 'satirize' instead. A natural reply is 'Ha, that's a good send-up.'

distinctions.note: Parody is a more formal or literary word for a work that imitates another, while send up is informal and spoken.
Mock is more hostile and direct, while send up often means a playful imitation that the target might enjoy.

examples.everyday: My brother does an impression of our dad, and he sends him up at every family dinner.
examples.professional: Mark sent up the vendor's buzzwords in his slide, and everyone laughed, though the client didn't find it funny.
examples.analytical: Satire sends up the pretensions of its targets by exaggerating their gestures until their hollowness becomes visible.

nuance.analogy: Like a funhouse mirror that stretches a face until its flaws are obvious, a send-up exaggerates someone until you see them clearly.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sendan, to cause to go; up from Old English up.
common_mistakes: Confusing send up with its literal meaning of sending something upward, as in sending a rocket up.
Using send up for serious criticism; it means parody, so it can sound unfair in a serious context.

senses.definition: A logical conclusion or consequence of facts.

core.definition: A conclusion that logically follows from the premises or facts given. In everyday English, it appears mostly in the phrase non sequitur.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SEK-. The second syllable is a short i, and the last syllable is an American r-colored schwa, so it does not end in an oh or ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in logic and debate. In conversation, the phrase non sequitur is used with mild criticism, meaning a remark that does not follow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sequitur mainly in logic, philosophy, law, and academic argument. In casual conversation, people almost always say non sequitur for a random, unrelated remark. Using sequitur alone in a casual setting would sound stiff or show-offy.

distinctions.note: A non sequitur is a conclusion that does not follow, which is a flaw, while a sequitur in the strict sense is a conclusion that does follow.
A consequence is any result of an event, while a sequitur is specifically a logical inference that follows from premises.

examples.everyday: His answer about the coffee was a total non sequitur, so I had no idea what he was talking about.
examples.professional: Your conclusion that churn is caused by pricing is not a sequitur from our data, since we have not controlled for contract length.
examples.analytical: The argument is valid only if the conclusion is a logical sequitur from its premises, not merely a plausible result of them.

nuance.analogy: A sequitur is like a staircase: each step must rest on the one below it, so the conclusion stands only if every earlier step is solid.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sequitur, meaning it follows, the third-person singular present of sequi, to follow.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'SEE-kwih-tur' with a long e, when the stress and the first vowel are short.
Using sequitur alone as a casual word for something unrelated; Americans say non sequitur in that situation.

sequitur.etymology: Latin *sequitur* (“it follows”), the third person form of *sequor* (“to follow”).

senses.definition: To separate and reserve something for a specific purpose.
senses.example: Plan to set aside three or four hours to see the museum.

senses.definition: To leave out of account; to omit or neglect.
senses.example: We will set aside the cost question for now and focus on the design.

senses.definition: To disagree with something and reject or overturn it.
senses.example: The senator set aside her colleague's proposal, arguing it ignored local farmers.

senses.definition: To declare something invalid or null and void.
senses.example: The judge set aside the verdict because the jury had been improperly instructed.

core.definition: To save or reserve something, such as money or time, for later use or a specific purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SIDE, and the first vowel of aside is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'uh-SIDE', not 'ah-SIDE'. In fast speech the t of set links into the next vowel, so it sounds like 'se-tuh-SIDE'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests planning and reserving something deliberately, though it can be negative when it means ignoring a problem.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly for saving money, time or space: 'I set aside twenty dollars every payday.' It also means putting a disagreement aside for now: 'Let's set our differences aside.' It is neutral enough for work, home and church. A natural reply is 'Smart idea' or 'Good plan.'

distinctions.note: Save means keep money or avoid waste; set aside emphasizes deliberately reserving something for a particular purpose.
Put aside usually means postpone something temporarily, while set aside often means reserving it for a goal or dismissing it on purpose.

examples.everyday: I try to set aside twenty dollars every payday for emergencies.
examples.professional: Let's set aside two hours on Thursday to review the model's error analysis.
examples.analytical: We must set aside the empirical question for now to examine the logical structure of the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like putting a dollar in a jar on the shelf: you are holding it back for a future purpose.
nuance.etymology: From set (Old English settan) and aside, from a- (on) plus side, meaning to one side.
common_mistakes: Saying 'set aside of money' or 'set aside from money'; the verb takes its object directly, as in 'set aside money'.
Treating set aside as mere saving; it often implies a deliberate decision to reserve something for a specific use.

senses.definition: To improve; to correct one's bad habits or behavior.
senses.example: He'd better shape up soon, or he'll fail the class.

senses.definition: To take shape; to transform into or become.
senses.example: The fog has vanished and it's shaping up to be a beautiful day.

senses.definition: To gesture or posture threateningly; to approach as if to fight; to pose to intimidate.
senses.example: The two men began to shape up, squaring their shoulders and glaring at each other.

core.definition: To improve one's behavior or performance, often after being warned that it is not acceptable.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on UP, not on shape. The vowel in up is short, like the 'u' of 'cup', and the final p is crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It is often said as a direct warning to someone who is not meeting expectations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'shape up' to a child, employee, or teammate who is misbehaving or performing poorly, often in the warning 'shape up or ship out.' It can also describe a plan or project that is developing well, as in 'the project is shaping up nicely.' A natural reply is 'You're right, I'll do better.'

distinctions.note: Straighten up can mean tidying or behaving well in general, while shape up usually means that someone's performance or conduct has been unacceptable and must improve.
Pull yourself together is said to someone recovering composure after emotional distress, not to someone whose work or habits need fixing.
Get your act together means to become organized and effective; shape up is more directly about changing bad behavior.

examples.everyday: Your brother has been skipping class for months, so his parents finally told him to shape up.
examples.professional: If your code keeps failing the review checks, you need to shape up before the next release.
examples.analytical: Calls for institutions to shape up often assume that reform is a matter of individual will rather than of structure.

nuance.analogy: Like a rough sketch that gradually becomes a finished drawing, shape up means that messy work begins to take a clear, acceptable form.
nuance.etymology: Combines shape with the particle up, which gives the sense of bringing something into a finished or acceptable condition.
common_mistakes: Stressing shape; the main stress belongs on up.
Using it as a polite request to a boss or client; it is a blunt demand and sounds harsh in formal settings.

senses.definition: To avoid, especially a duty, responsibility, etc. to stay away from.
To evade an obligation; to avoid the performance of duty, as by running away.
senses.example: If you have a job, don't shirk from it by staying off work.

senses.definition: To procure by petty fraud and trickery; to obtain by mean solicitation.
senses.example: The old swindler would shirk free drinks from anyone willing to hear his sob story.

senses.definition: One who shirks, who avoids a duty or responsibility.
senses.example: Nobody wanted to work with him because he was a chronic shirk who vanished before deadlines.

senses.definition: The unforgivable sin of association (claiming something or someone can share in the oneness of God).
senses.example: The council condemned the heretic's teaching as shirk, a claim that a creature could share God's oneness.

core.definition: To avoid a duty, task or responsibility that you should do, often by making excuses or hiding.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the rhotic 'er' sound, like the vowel in 'work', so say it as 'SHURK' with one syllable. Don't add a vowel after the r.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests laziness or cowardice in avoiding one's responsibilities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use shirk in work, school and family settings to criticize someone who avoids a job, such as 'He always shirks his share of the cleaning'. It is direct and a little judgmental, so use it with care. The phrase 'shirk responsibility' is common, and the noun is rare.

distinctions.note: Dodge is more informal and suggests a quick, clever avoidance, while shirk suggests a deliberate failure to do what you should.
Avoid is neutral and general, while shirk implies that the avoided thing was your duty.

examples.everyday: My roommate always shirks the dishes, so I end up doing them.
examples.professional: Several team members shirked the code review, so the release got delayed.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's ethics would condemn anyone who shirks the civic duties that make a good life possible.

nuance.analogy: To shirk a duty is like leaving a heavy box in the hallway for someone else to carry.
nuance.etymology: Probably from 'shirk' (a sneak, a parasite), of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using 'shirk' as a noun meaning a person who avoids work; the noun is 'shirker'.
Using 'shirk from' instead of 'shirk' alone.

senses.definition: A difficulty in breathing.

core.definition: A difficulty in breathing, where you feel you cannot get enough air. It is a common symptom that doctors ask about.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BREATH, the noun, and 'of' is a weak 'uhv'. Learners often say 'breathe' with a /ð/ sound, but the noun 'breath' ends in a voiceless /θ/ like 'think'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals a health concern, so it is serious when it comes on suddenly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in medical settings, on forms, or when describing symptoms to a doctor or 911 dispatcher. In casual speech people more often say 'I can't catch my breath' or 'I'm having trouble breathing.' If the shortness of breath starts suddenly or comes with chest pain, Americans call 911 right away.

distinctions.note: 'Out of breath' is temporary and usually follows exertion, such as running up stairs, while shortness of breath can happen at rest and may signal illness.
Breathlessness is a close synonym that is less clinical and more descriptive; the medical phrase is shortness of breath.

collocations: chest pain and shortness of breath

examples.everyday: My dad got some shortness of breath after climbing the stairs, so he sat down and called his doctor.
examples.professional: Please record any shortness of breath or chest pain in the incident report before the patient is transferred.
examples.analytical: Shortness of breath is a subjective report, so clinicians must weigh it against objective measures such as oxygen saturation.

nuance.analogy: Like a garden hose with a kink in it: water still flows, but not enough reaches the end.
nuance.etymology: 'Short' from Old English sceort and 'breath' from Old English bræth; the phrase is a compound description.
common_mistakes: Saying 'short breath' instead of 'shortness of breath'.
Using 'shortness of breath' for ordinary tiredness after exercise; 'out of breath' is more natural there.
Pronouncing 'breath' with a /ð/ ending like the verb 'breathe'.

senses.definition: A loud burst of voice or voices; a violent and sudden outcry, especially that of a multitude expressing joy, triumph, exultation, anger, or great effort.
senses.example: give out a shout

senses.definition: A greeting, name-check or other mention, for example on a radio or TV program.
senses.example: Next up the new single from Beyoncé, but first a shout to Barry Bloggins and his wife Belinda...

senses.definition: A suggestion; an idea.
senses.example: Thanks for the shout about the new hiking trail, we loved it.

senses.definition: To utter a sudden and loud cry, as in joy, triumph, exultation or anger, or to attract attention, to animate others, etc.
senses.example: Mom shouted to us to come sit at the table.

senses.definition: To utter with a shout; to cry; to shout out.
senses.example: They shouted his name to get his attention.

senses.definition: To forcefully attract attention or proclaim one’s presence.
senses.example: The guard had to shout to be heard above the crowd at the stadium.

senses.definition: To post a text message (for example, email) in upper case, regarded as the electronic messaging equivalent of oral shouting.
senses.example: Please don't shout in the chat room.

core.definition: To say something very loudly, usually to express emotion or to get someone's attention.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the 'ow' of 'out', a diphthong that glides from 'ah' to 'oo'. The final 't' is light, and do not confuse it with 'shoot'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can express joy or excitement, but it is often used for anger or rudeness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'shout out' for a public thanks or greeting, as in 'Shout out to my mom!' Shouting at someone in anger is common, but 'yell' is even more typical for angry speech. In a restaurant or office, shouting across the room may seem rude.

distinctions.note: 'Yell' is more typical for anger, urgency or warnings, while 'shout' can also express joy or a call for attention.
A scream is higher-pitched and more intense, often from fear or pain, while a shout is loud but usually voiced.
A call can be spoken at a normal volume over a distance; a shout is louder and more forceful.

examples.everyday: Don't shout at the waiter, he can hear you just fine.
examples.professional: Please don't shout across the room during the call; just unmute and speak into the mic.
examples.analytical: Political slogans often shout what they cannot argue, substituting volume for evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like turning up a speaker to full volume: the sound is louder, but not necessarily clearer.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English shouten; the origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'shout' with 'shoot' because of similar spelling.
Using 'shout' for a quiet call; Americans would say 'call out' or 'say'.
Saying 'shout out to' in formal writing where 'thank' is better.

senses.definition: A perforated nozzle that showers water on a bather, sometimes in adjustable patterns.
senses.example: The new showerhead sprays a gentle mist that makes the bathroom feel like a spa.

senses.definition: A part of a coffeemaker for dispersing water evenly over the grounds.
senses.example: Clean the showerhead under the coffeemaker weekly so the water flows evenly over the grounds.

core.definition: The part of a shower that sprays water, usually a round fixture attached to the wall pipe.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle vowel reduced. The compound has a secondary stress on head, so say the final syllable with a short 'ed' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use showerhead for the nozzle, and the word is common in home repair, plumbing and product shopping. It is one word in standard American spelling. Saying 'shower head' in a casual way is also understood, but showerhead is the standard form.

distinctions.note: A faucet controls water at a sink or tub, while a showerhead sprays water in a shower.
Shower head as two words is a common variant, but showerhead is the standard American form in dictionaries and product listings.

examples.everyday: The water pressure is weak, so I think the showerhead needs cleaning.
examples.professional: The contractor recommended a low-flow showerhead to reduce water use in the building.
examples.analytical: The showerhead is a small device, but its design determines the pattern and pressure of the water that touches the body.

nuance.analogy: Like the sprinkler head on a garden hose, but mounted above your head.
nuance.etymology: From shower and head, referring to the part that sends water down.
common_mistakes: Writing 'shower head' as two words in formal writing where showerhead is standard.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

conversation.text: We put in a new showerhead, and the water pressure is so much better.
The showerhead is dripping even when it's off.
Soak the showerhead in vinegar to clean the buildup.

senses.definition: A performance or segment of a theatrical production that induces a positive audience reaction strong enough to pause the production.
senses.example: Her solo in the second act was a showstopper, and the audience applauded for nearly five minutes.

senses.definition: Any impediment that prevents all further progress.
senses.example: The missing permit was a showstopper for the construction crew, halting work on the entire site.

senses.definition: A software bug that must be fixed before any further development is possible.
senses.example: The login crash is a showstopper, so we can't ship the release until engineers fix it.

core.definition: Something, often a performance, so impressive that the audience applauds loudly and stops the show; also a major problem that halts progress.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'SHOH', and the last syllable is a light, r-colored 'er'. Do not stress 'stop' too strongly, and do not add a 't' sound between the 'p' and 'er'.

nuance.connotation: Positive for an impressive performance, and negative for a serious problem that stops progress; context shows which meaning applies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'showstopper' informally for an amazing performance, a dish, or a product that wows people, as in 'her solo was a showstopper.' In business and technology, it means a problem that must be fixed before anything else can move forward. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: A highlight is the best part of something, while a showstopper is so impressive that the event pauses for applause.
A blocker is any obstacle, while a showstopper is an especially serious obstacle that stops all progress.
A hit is a popular success, while a showstopper is an impressive moment that stands out in a performance.

examples.everyday: Grandma's apple pie was a showstopper at Thanksgiving, and everyone asked for the recipe.
examples.professional: The authentication bug is a showstopper, so we can't release the app until the team fixes it.
examples.analytical: The incarnation, for many theologians, is the showstopper of the whole argument, because it changes how one understands God and humanity.

nuance.analogy: A showstopper is like a bridge that is washed out in the middle of a road trip; you cannot keep going until it is repaired.
nuance.etymology: From 'show' and 'stopper', meaning something that stops the show.
common_mistakes: Using 'showstopper' only for performances; it is also used for software and project problems.
Writing it as two words, 'show stopper', which is less common in American writing.

senses.definition: Drooling; the flow of excess saliva from the mouth.

core.definition: Excessive drooling; the flow of excess saliva out of the mouth, usually caused by a medical or neurological condition.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -rhea syllable, and the middle syllables are quick and reduced. Don't add an extra syllable or say 'see-uh-LOR-ee-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical; it describes a symptom without judgment, though it can feel blunt when used about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sialorrhea mainly in medicine, neurology and speech therapy, and in clinical discussions of conditions like Parkinson's disease or ALS. In everyday talk people say drooling or excessive drooling instead. Using sialorrhea with a family member or friend would sound overly clinical, so use it in a doctor's office or a medical setting.

distinctions.note: Drooling is the everyday word used by most Americans; sialorrhea is the technical term for the same condition.
Ptyalism is an older medical word for excess saliva that is nearly interchangeable with sialorrhea, but sialorrhea is more common in current American medicine.

examples.everyday: My dad has trouble with drooling from his Parkinson's, so the doctor is looking at treatments for the sialorrhea.
examples.professional: The clinical trial tracked sialorrhea severity in patients with ALS using a standard rating scale.
examples.analytical: The authors argue that sialorrhea in neurological disease often reflects impaired swallowing rather than true oversecretion of saliva.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that won't shut off, except the leak is in the mouth.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sialon (saliva) and rhoia (a flow).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, such as 'SY-uh-luh-ree-uh' with stress at the start.
Using sialorrhea in casual conversation, where drooling is the natural word.

senses.definition: A paid personal day intended to be used due to illness either for recuperation or medical treatment.
senses.example: I took a sick day yesterday because my fever was too high to get out of bed.

core.definition: A paid day off from work for an illness, or a day you stay home from school or work because you are sick.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'day' in this compound noun. 'Sick' is short and has a clear k at the end, so don't let it sound like 'sick' with a long i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sick day for a day off work or school due to illness, often as a paid benefit. You might say 'I'm taking a sick day' when calling your manager. Some companies have separate sick leave policies, so 'sick leave' is also common in HR contexts.

distinctions.note: Sick leave is the policy or benefit, often in longer or formal terms, while sick day is the single day of absence.
A vacation day is planned leave for rest or travel, while a sick day is taken because of illness.

examples.everyday: I'm running a fever, so I'm taking a sick day and staying in bed.
examples.professional: Hi Sarah, I'm taking a sick day today, so I'll be offline until tomorrow morning.
examples.analytical: Paid sick days are often studied as a public health policy because they affect whether sick workers stay home and avoid spreading illness.

nuance.analogy: A sick day is like a pause button for your job: it stops work for a day so your body can recover.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a sick day off' in casual speech, which is redundant but sometimes heard; 'a sick day' is enough.
Writing 'sick-day' as one word or without a hyphen when it modifies a noun, such as 'sick-day policy.'

conversation.text: I'm taking a sick day; I can barely get out of bed.
How many sick days do you get a year?
I used all my sick days when the kids had the flu.

senses.definition: To log off; to stop using a computer, radio, etc. especially, to stop talking.
senses.example: He finished the conversation and signed off.

senses.definition: To cease broadcasting a radio or television signal, usually at the end of a broadcasting day.
senses.example: Before he signed off the radio station for the night, the disc jockey played the National Anthem.

senses.definition: To give one's official approval to something for which it is needed, especially by a signature.
senses.example: Once the vice-president signs off on the project, we can start construction.

senses.definition: To use a valediction, such as the end of a letter or broadcast.

core.definition: To give formal approval to something, usually by signing your name, so that it can move forward.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'OFF' as the main word; 'on' is weak, so it sounds like 'un' or 'in'. Link the words smoothly so it sounds like 'sine-OFF-un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is a normal workplace phrase that shows an official decision was made.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sign off on' constantly at work, for budgets, designs, invoices, and reports, often in meetings or emails. Someone might say 'Has Sarah signed off on the budget yet?' A natural reply is 'Yes, she signed off on it this morning' or 'Not yet, we're waiting for her approval.' Do not confuse it with the broadcasting or computer meanings, which are less common in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: 'Approve' is the general word for accepting something, while 'sign off on' implies a formal, documented final step, often with a signature.
'Agree to' can be informal and personal, while 'sign off on' usually refers to a formal decision that carries institutional weight.

collocations: get someone to sign off on it

examples.everyday: My landlord still has to sign off on the lease change before we can move the date.
examples.professional: Legal needs to sign off on the vendor contract before we can start the pilot next week.
examples.analytical: Institutions often require a formal authority to sign off on a decision, which makes accountability clear but can slow the process.

nuance.analogy: Signing off on something is like stamping a package 'approved' before it leaves the warehouse: it's the last official step.
nuance.etymology: Sign comes from Latin 'signum' (mark, token) and off comes from Old English 'of', meaning away from.
common_mistakes: Dropping the 'on', saying 'sign off the budget' instead of 'sign off on the budget'.
Using 'sign off' alone to mean approve in formal writing, where 'sign off on' is clearer.

conversation.text: The director has to sign off on the budget.
Did legal sign off on the contract?
I'll sign off on the design once the colors are fixed.

senses.definition: Having a noticeable amount of silt.
senses.example: The silty river needed its channel dredged periodically to remain navigable.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of silt.
senses.example: After the flood, the riverbed was covered with a thick, silty layer that smelled of wet earth.

core.definition: Containing or covered with silt, or having the fine, powdery texture of silt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is a light ee sound, so it sounds like 'SIL-tee', not 'sil-TEE'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is descriptive and mostly used for soil, water, or sediment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use silty mainly in soil science, farming, geology, and outdoor or environmental contexts, such as describing a riverbank or a field. It is rarely used for people or abstract things. In casual talk people might say muddy or sandy instead.

distinctions.note: Muddy describes wet, sticky ground in general, while silty specifically describes soil or water with fine particles.
Sandy means gritty, coarse particles are present, while silty means finer, smoother particles dominate.

examples.everyday: The garden soil is silty, so it holds water well but drains slowly after heavy rain.
examples.professional: We need to test the silty samples from the north field before we decide on the irrigation plan.
examples.analytical: The silty deposits in the delta show how the river's flow slowed over centuries.

nuance.analogy: Like powdered flour that has been mixed with water: smooth, fine, and easy to spread.
nuance.etymology: Derived from silt with the adjective suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using silty for people or feelings, which sounds odd in American English.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes it sound unnatural.

senses.definition: Strangely; oddly.
senses.example: He behaved most singularly when we met him last night.

senses.definition: Extremely; remarkably.
In the singular number; in terms of a single thing.
senses.example: The noun is used singularly in this context, referring to one specific account only.

senses.definition: Solely; only; uniquely.
senses.example: She was singularly qualified for the job, with a rare mix of statistics and theology.

core.definition: In a remarkable, unusual, or extreme way; to an unusual degree.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle 'ular' is reduced to 'yuh-ler,' and the ending is pronounced 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral or positive when it describes qualities such as skill or fit, and negative when it describes failure, as in 'singularly unhelpful.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'singularly' mainly in formal writing, reviews, and professional prose, as in 'singularly well-suited.' In everyday speech it can sound stiff, so people often say 'especially' or 'remarkably' instead. Don't confuse it with 'singly,' which means one at a time.

distinctions.note: Singly means one at a time, while singularly means unusually or remarkably, so the two words are not interchangeable.
Especially is more common and natural in speech, while singularly is more formal and emphatic.
Uniquely means in a way that is unlike anything else, while singularly emphasizes an extreme degree of a quality.

examples.everyday: That pizza was singularly bad, honestly; I've never had worse.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was singularly well-suited to our tight timeline and budget.
examples.analytical: The author's argument is singularly persuasive because it anticipates every serious objection to its central premise.

nuance.analogy: Singularly is like a spotlight on one quality, making it stand out far more than usual.
nuance.etymology: From 'singular' (Latin singularis, 'single') plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using 'singularly' to mean 'singly' or 'one at a time'; the two words have different meanings.
Using 'singularly' in casual speech where 'especially' or 'remarkably' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: A thin, broad piece cut off.
senses.example: a slice of bacon; a slice of cheese; a slice of bread

senses.definition: A broad, thin piece of plaster.
A piece of pizza, shaped like a sector of a circle.
senses.example: She cut the pizza and took a slice before the game started.

senses.definition: That which is thin and broad.
senses.example: A thin slice of morning light fell across the kitchen floor.

senses.definition: A knife with a thin, broad blade for taking up or serving fish; also, a spatula for spreading anything, as paint or ink.
senses.example: My grandmother set out a silver fish slice for serving the salmon at dinner.

senses.definition: An amount of anything.
senses.example: Each of us got a slice of the profits from the project.

senses.definition: A salver, platter, or tray.
senses.example: The waiter balanced the glasses on a silver slice as he crossed the dining room.

senses.definition: A plate of iron with a handle, forming a kind of chisel, or a spadelike implement, variously proportioned, and used for various purposes, as for stripping the planking from a vessel's side, for cutting blubber from a whale, or for stirring a fire of coals; a slice bar; a peel; a fire shovel.
senses.example: The blacksmith kept a long iron slice by the forge for moving hot coals.

senses.definition: One of the wedges by which the cradle and the ship are lifted clear of the building blocks to prepare for launching.
senses.example: The shipwrights drove the wooden slices under the cradle before launching the hull.

senses.definition: A shot that (for the right-handed player) curves unintentionally to the right. See fade, hook, draw.
senses.example: My drive took a slice into the trees on the right side of the fairway.

senses.definition: A hawk's or falcon's dropping which squirts at an angle other than vertical. (See mute.)
senses.example: The falconer checked the perch for any slice that might signal the hawk was ill.

senses.definition: A contiguous portion of an array.
senses.example: The function returns a slice of the array starting at index two.

senses.definition: A removable sliding bottom to a galley.
senses.example: We pulled the removable slice from the galley to reach the bilge beneath.

senses.definition: A kind of cut shot where the bat makes an obtuse angle with the batter.
senses.example: The batter tried a slice past point, but the ball bounced off the edge.

senses.definition: A section of image taken of an internal organ using MRI (magnetic resonance imaging), CT (computed tomography), or various forms of x-ray.
senses.example: The radiologist reviewed each slice of the scan to look for a tumor.

senses.definition: To cut into slices.
senses.example: Slice the cheese thinly.

senses.definition: To cut with an edge using a drawing motion.
senses.example: The knife left sliced his arm.

senses.definition: To clear (e.g. a fire, or the grate bars of a furnace) by means of a slice bar.
senses.example: Every morning the stoker sliced the furnace grate to clear out ash.

senses.definition: To hit the shuttlecock with the racket at an angle, causing it to move sideways and downwards.
senses.example: She sliced the shuttlecock sideways over the net, catching her opponent off guard.

senses.definition: To hit a shot that slices (travels from left to right for a right-handed player).
senses.example: He sliced his drive badly and lost the ball in the woods.

senses.definition: To angle the blade so that it goes too deeply into the water when starting to take a stroke.
To kick the ball so that it goes in an unintended direction, at too great an angle or too high.
To hit the ball with a stroke that causes a spin, resulting in the ball swerving or staying low after a bounce.
Having the properties of a slice knot.

core.definition: A thin, flat piece cut from a larger food, such as bread, cheese, meat, or pizza.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable with a long i sound. Avoid adding a vowel before the s, as in "es-lice," and keep the final s crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and pleasant in food contexts; it suggests a portion that is easy to share.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "slice" for bread, cake, pie, cheese, and especially pizza, where a slice is a single triangular piece. Ordering "a slice" at a pizza place is very common and casual. For a whole loaf, people say "a slice of bread," not "a piece of bread."

distinctions.note: "Piece" is general for any part, while "slice" specifically means a thin, flat portion cut through.
A chunk is thick and irregular, while a slice is thin and even.

examples.everyday: Could I get one more slice of pepperoni pizza, please?
examples.professional: Please put a slice of the quarterly summary on the first page so everyone sees the key number.
examples.analytical: Each slice of the dataset reveals only part of the pattern, which is why we must examine the whole.

nuance.analogy: Like cutting a loaf into even pieces, a slice is one thin portion taken from a whole.
nuance.etymology: From Old French esclice, a splinter, from a Germanic root related to slit.
common_mistakes: Saying "a piece of bread" for a slice of bread, which sounds unnatural to Americans.
Confusing the noun "slice" with the verb pronunciation, which is the same sound.

slice.etymology: From Middle English *sclise*, *sklise*, from Old French *esclice*, *esclis* (“a piece split off”), deverbal of *esclicer*, *esclicier* (“to splinter, split up”), from **slitjan* (“to split up”), from Proto-Germanic **slitjaną*, from Proto-Germanic…

conversation.text: Can you slice the bread for the sandwiches?
I'll have a slice of pizza, please.
There's some left. Want a slice of cake?

senses.definition: A small request for help.

core.definition: A minor request for help, often used politely when asking someone to do something simple.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on favor, the second word, which is the main stress in the phrase. Small has a soft l at the end, and favor is pronounced fay-ver with the r light but clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive and polite. It makes a request sound minor and considerate, which is helpful in everyday conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say can you do me a small favor? when asking a neighbor, coworker, or friend for something simple, such as watching the mail or picking up a package. A natural reply is sure, no problem or of course. Saying the phrase too often can sound like a way of creating obligation, so use it when the request really is small.

distinctions.note: A favor alone is a broader term; small favor specifically signals that the request is minor and easy.
A big favor signals a significant or inconvenient request, and people often apologize before asking for it.

examples.everyday: Hey, could you do me a small favor and grab some milk on your way home?
examples.professional: Could you do me a small favor and send the revised slides before the call?
examples.analytical: A small favor can reveal the moral structure of a relationship, since it creates a debt that both parties recognize.

nuance.analogy: A small favor is like a light tap on the shoulder: it asks for attention without creating a heavy burden.
nuance.etymology: Favor comes from Old French favour, from Latin favor, meaning goodwill; small is from Old English smæl.
common_mistakes: Saying a small favour, with British spelling, in American writing.
Using do a favor for me when the natural American phrase is do me a favor.

conversation.text: Can I ask you a small favor? Could you feed my cat this weekend?
It's just a small favor, but it would really help me out.
"I have a small favor to ask." "Sure, what's up?"

senses.definition: To burn slowly, giving off smoke but with little to no flame.
senses.example: The remains of the bonfire were left to smolder for hours.

senses.definition: To show signs of repressed anger or suppressed mental turmoil or other strong emotion, such as passion.
senses.example: Though he smiled politely, his resentment continued to smolder beneath the surface during the meeting.

senses.definition: To exist in a suppressed or hidden state.
senses.example: Old grievances continued to smolder quietly in the family long after the lawsuit ended.

senses.definition: The act of smoldering or something that smolders.
senses.example: The smolder from the abandoned campfire woke us before dawn, filling the tent with smoke.

core.definition: To burn slowly with smoke but little flame, or to hold a strong feeling such as anger in a hidden, intense way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The 'l' is clear, and the ending is a flapped or softened 'er' sound, so it sounds like 'SMOHL-der'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing fire; negative or tense when describing anger or resentment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use smolder for a fire or cigarette that burns slowly, and for hidden anger: 'He smoldered during the meeting.' The British spelling is smoulder, which is less common in American writing. Americans also use it for a suppressed passion or attraction, sometimes with a playful tone.

distinctions.note: Smoke is the visible gas or particles; smolder is the slow burning that produces them.
Burn can mean any flaming fire; smolder means slow burning without much flame.

examples.everyday: The campfire was smoldering, so I threw more water on it before we left.
examples.professional: The team has been smoldering over the reorg since spring, and it finally came out in the retro.
examples.analytical: Resentment that smolders beneath polite conversation can distort judgment more than open conflict does.

nuance.analogy: A smoldering fire is like a coal under ash: it looks quiet, but heat is still building underneath.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English smolderen, to smoke without flame; the exact early origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Writing 'smoulder' in American writing; the standard American spelling is smolder.
Confusing smolder with smother, which means to cover or suffocate.

smolder.etymology: From Middle English *smolderen* (“to suffocate, stifle”), from Middle English *smolder* (“smoke, smoky vapour”), ultimately from **smolōn* (“to burn, glow, fume, smoulder”).

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the sun; proceeding from the sun.
senses.example: solar light

senses.definition: Measured by the progress or revolution of the sun in the ecliptic; as, the solar year.
senses.example: The solar year is about 365 days, measured by Earth's orbit around the sun.

senses.definition: Produced by the action of the sun, or peculiarly affected by its influence.
senses.example: Sunburn is a solar injury, caused by ultraviolet radiation from the sun.

senses.definition: Employing solar power.
senses.example: a solar furnace

senses.definition: Ellipsis of solar energy.
A fictional currency.
senses.example: In the novel, the merchants of Vega accepted solar as payment instead of gold.

senses.definition: (historical) A loft or upper chamber forming the private accommodation of the head of the household in a medieval hall; a garret room.
senses.example: In the old manor, the solar was where the master slept above the great hall.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Of or relating to the sun, or powered or produced by energy from the sun.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the final -ar a weak American R-colored vowel, as in 'sooner', not 'ar' as in 'car'. It has two syllables, not three.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when used for clean energy. Technically neutral in science contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solar most often for solar panels, solar power and solar energy in homes, businesses and policy discussions. In casual speech they may say 'solar' alone for a solar-powered device, but usually add the noun. In astronomy and physics, solar is standard and precise.

distinctions.note: Sunny describes weather or a bright day. Solar describes something related to the sun's energy or its physical properties.
Lunar relates to the moon, while solar relates to the sun. The two are often paired in calendars and astronomy.
Photovoltaic is a technical term for converting light to electricity. Solar is broader and includes heating and other sun-based uses.

examples.everyday: We put solar panels on the roof last year, and our electric bill has dropped a lot.
examples.professional: The data pipeline ingests solar generation forecasts from three regional providers every morning.
examples.analytical: The solar year, unlike the lunar calendar, is tied to the earth's orbit around the sun, which is why the seasons stay aligned with it.

nuance.analogy: Like a sunflower turning toward light: solar energy is what something draws from the sun.
nuance.etymology: From Latin solaris, meaning of the sun, from sol, the sun.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the last syllable as a full AR sound, as in 'car', instead of the weak American R sound.
Confusing solar with sooner or solace; the vowels and stress differ.

solar.etymology: From Late Middle English *solar*, from Latin *sōlāris*, from *sōl* (“sun”), from Proto-Indo-European **sóh₂wl̥* (“sun”).

senses.definition: In a solicitous manner.

core.definition: In a caring and attentive way that shows concern for someone's comfort, health or feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the ending -ously is reduced to 'us-lee'. Avoid saying 'so-LEE-sit-ous-lee' with extra stress on the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests kindness and attentiveness, though it can sound slightly excessive or ironic if overdone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use solicitously in writing or formal speech to describe someone who is attentive to another person's needs, such as a host or nurse. In everyday talk people more often say kindly or with concern. It is natural in a description of a scene, but not common in casual conversation.

distinctions.note: Solicitously means caring about someone else's well-being, while anxiously means worried, often about one's own outcome.
Attentively means paying close attention, while solicitously adds a sense of warmth and concern for the other person.

examples.everyday: Our waiter asked solicitously whether everything was okay with our meal, and he brought extra napkins without being asked.
examples.professional: Our manager asked solicitously how the team was handling the new deadline, which made everyone feel supported.
examples.analytical: The essay treats its reader solicitously, anticipating objections before they are raised, so that its argument feels almost pastoral.

nuance.analogy: Acting solicitously is like a good host who notices an empty glass and refills it before the guest has to ask.
nuance.etymology: From solicitous, from Latin sollicitus, meaning anxious or careful, with -ly added in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing solicitously with solicit, which is a verb meaning to ask for something.
Stressing the last syllable, saying 'suh-lis-ih-TUS-lee'.
Using it to mean worried about one's own problems, when it means caring about another person.

senses.definition: In one way or another; in a way not yet known or explained; by some means.
senses.example: This problem has to be tackled somehow.

core.definition: In a way that is not known, not clear, or not yet explained; by some means, one way or another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUM, and make 'how' a diphthong like 'cow'. The 'h' is clearly pronounced and should not be dropped, so say 'SUM-how'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when describing a successful result ('We somehow finished on time'); neutral or frustrated when describing confusion or loss.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'somehow' a lot in casual conversation to describe something they cannot explain or that happened despite the odds. It often expresses surprise or relief. In formal writing, it can sound vague, so writers usually explain how something happened.

distinctions.note: 'Somehow or other' is more casual and emphasizes that the method does not matter.
'Anyhow' means 'in any case' or 'anyway' as a transition, not 'by some unknown means'.

examples.everyday: I don't know how, but I somehow lost my keys again this morning.
examples.professional: The team somehow shipped the release on time, even after the outage on Tuesday.
examples.analytical: Augustine struggles to explain how evil somehow exists within a creation that God made good.

nuance.analogy: 'Somehow' is like a river finding its way around a rock: the route is not visible at first, but the water still gets through.
nuance.etymology: From 'some', meaning 'a certain', combined with 'how'.
common_mistakes: Using 'somehow' to mean 'somewhat' ('It's somehow better'); 'somehow' refers to a method, not a degree.
Pronouncing it as 'SUM-ho', dropping the 'w' sound in the second syllable.

senses.definition: The state or condition of being soundless.

core.definition: The state of having no sound at all; complete silence or stillness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, SOUND. Say the d lightly or not at all, and keep the final -ness unstressed and short, like 'nuss'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can suggest peace, emptiness or tension depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in conversation. It appears in literary, descriptive or academic writing, where it names the quality of being silent. In speech, people usually say 'the silence' or 'how quiet it was' instead.

distinctions.note: Silence is the common everyday word for the absence of sound. Soundlessness is a more abstract, literary noun for that quality.
Stillness refers to a lack of motion as well as sound. Soundlessness refers only to the lack of sound.

examples.professional: The soundlessness of the server room made the faint fan noise stand out.
examples.analytical: Some mystics describe prayer as a soundlessness in which words give way to presence.

nuance.analogy: Like the hush inside a sealed jar, where you notice that nothing at all is moving.
nuance.etymology: From soundless, plus the noun suffix -ness from Old English -nes.
common_mistakes: Confusing soundlessness with silence in everyday speech; Americans more often say silence or quiet.
Pronouncing the noun with stress on the final syllable; the stress stays on SOUND.

senses.definition: Speaking of which; relatedly, used to introduce a related topic.
senses.example: Speaking of dinner, have you tried that new Thai place on Fifth Street?

senses.definition: Synonym of speak of the devil.
senses.example: A: I wish Maria had come. B: Speaking of! Here she is!

core.definition: Used to introduce a new topic that relates to what was just mentioned, meaning 'that reminds me'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPEE. The word 'of' is reduced to a weak 'uv' sound, and the final 'ing' is a light 'ing' with no hard 'g'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a friendly transition in conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'speaking of' casually to shift to a related subject, such as 'Speaking of vacation, did you book the flights?' It is informal, so it is natural in conversation and emails to friends but less common in formal reports. A natural reply is to continue with the new topic.

distinctions.note: Speaking of which is a more emphatic version, used when the new topic is directly connected to the last one, as a response to a concrete reminder.
On that note usually closes a topic or moves to a related one, often in a more formal or meeting context.

examples.everyday: Speaking of pizza, do you want to order some for dinner?
examples.professional: Speaking of the Q3 report, can you send me the final numbers by Friday?
examples.analytical: Speaking of moral responsibility, the author raises questions about who bears the cost of unintended harm.

nuance.analogy: It works like a signpost on a road, pointing to a nearby turn in the conversation.
nuance.etymology: From the present participle of speak, plus of, used in conversational transitions.
common_mistakes: Using it when the topics are not related at all, which can confuse listeners.
Saying 'speak about' in place of 'speaking of'.

conversation.text: Speaking of food, has anyone tried the new burger place downtown?
"My brother's in town this week." "Oh, speaking of brothers, how's Danny?"
Speaking of vacations, are you guys still going to Mexico?

senses.definition: An obsolete term for specific heat capacity.
senses.example: My grandfather's old chemistry book used specific heat for what we now call heat capacity.

core.definition: In physics and chemistry, the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of one unit of mass of a substance by one degree.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'heat,' with a lighter stress on 'spe' in 'specific.' The 'i' in 'specific' is short, and 'heat' is a long 'eet' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It has no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans still use 'specific heat' in physics, chemistry, and engineering classes, so the term is not obsolete as the input suggested. Many textbooks and engineers say 'specific heat capacity' for clarity, and the two terms are used interchangeably. In everyday talk, Americans rarely use it.

distinctions.note: 'Heat capacity' refers to the heat needed to raise the temperature of an entire object; 'specific heat' refers to the same quantity per unit mass.

examples.everyday: Water has a high specific heat, which is why the lake stays cool well into summer.
examples.professional: We need the specific heat of the coolant to size the heat exchanger correctly.
examples.analytical: The derivation shows how specific heat depends on the degrees of freedom of the molecules.

nuance.analogy: Like the amount of food a person needs to gain one pound, it measures how much energy a material takes to warm up.
nuance.etymology: 'Specific' from Latin specificus, combined with 'heat' from Old English hǣtu.
common_mistakes: Treating it as obsolete, since American science courses use it regularly
Confusing it with 'heat' alone, which refers to thermal energy in transit

senses.definition: Of, or pertaining to, spectres; ghostly.
senses.example: The spectral chain-rattling and moans gave me the chills.

senses.definition: Of, or pertaining to, spectra; classified according to frequency or wavelength (of light, etc.).
senses.example: The astronomer used a spectral analysis to determine the star's surface temperature.

senses.definition: On the spectrum; spectrumy.

core.definition: Ghostly, eerie, or pale, like a specter or an apparition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'tr' blends into an American r, and the final 'l' is a dark l, so do not add an extra vowel between the r and the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests eeriness or something faint and unreal, though in science it is a neutral technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spectral' mainly in literary description, horror, or art criticism to mean ghostly or pale. In science and mathematics, the word refers to a spectrum, as in 'spectral analysis.' In everyday talk people more often say 'ghostly' or 'eerie,' so 'spectral' sounds elevated.

distinctions.note: Ghostly is the everyday word for resembling a ghost, while spectral is more formal and can also describe spectra in science.
Eerie describes a feeling of strange unease, while spectral refers to something ghost-like in appearance or a spectrum in technical use.

examples.everyday: The old lighthouse looked spectral in the fog, and we were glad to get back to the car.
examples.professional: The spectral analysis showed a strong absorption line, which tells us the sample contains hydrogen.
examples.analytical: Derrida's language of the spectral returns to the question of what haunts the present and cannot be fully present itself.

nuance.analogy: A spectral figure is like a photograph that has faded until only a pale outline of a person remains.
nuance.etymology: From Latin spectrum, 'appearance, image,' from specere, 'to look at.'
common_mistakes: Using 'spectral' in casual speech for 'ghostly,' which can sound too formal.
Confusing 'spectral' with 'spectrum' and using the adjective where the noun is needed.

senses.definition: A stopwatch with two second hands, each of which may be stopped separately to time the intervals of a race by a sportsperson, or to time more than one sportsperson.
senses.example: The coach used a split-second stopwatch to record each runner's lap times separately.

senses.definition: A fraction of a second; hence a very short time period; an instant, a moment.

core.definition: A very brief moment, an instant, a fraction of a second.

pronunciation.tip: Give 'split' secondary stress and 'SEK' primary stress. Reduce the second syllable of 'second' to a schwa, so it sounds like 'SEK-und,' not 'SEK-ond.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes time and speed, and it often suggests urgency or quick reaction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'in a split second' to describe something happening almost instantly, as in a car accident or a quick decision. It is also common as an adjective, as in 'a split-second decision.' The rare stopwatch sense is mainly historical or specialized, so the everyday meaning is the one to learn first.

distinctions.note: 'Instant' is the broader and more common word for a short moment, while 'split-second' emphasizes an extremely brief time, often in a quick reaction.
'Moment' is more general and can refer to a longer period, while 'split-second' suggests a nearly unmeasurable time.

examples.everyday: I almost hit the brake, but I reacted in a split second.
examples.professional: The system needs split-second timing to keep the sensor data aligned.
examples.analytical: Moral judgment is rarely a split-second matter, since it depends on reflection and character formed over time.

nuance.analogy: Like a camera shutter snapping open and shut in an instant.
nuance.etymology: Compound of split (divided) and second (a unit of time, from Latin secunda, following division of the hour).
common_mistakes: Writing 'split second' without the hyphen when used as an adjective.
Saying 'in a split of a second' instead of the standard 'in a split second.'
Using it for a long time period, since it always refers to a very brief moment.

senses.definition: The quality of being spontaneous.
Spontaneous behavior.
senses.example: Her spontaneity delighted the children, who never knew what she would do next.

senses.definition: The tendency to undergo change, characteristic of both animal and vegetable organisms, and not restrained or checked by the environment.
senses.example: Some early theories attributed the spontaneity of living organisms to an inner, self-directed vital force.

senses.definition: The tendency to activity of muscular tissue, including the voluntary muscles, when in a state of healthful vigor and refreshment.
senses.example: The physiology lecture described the spontaneity of smooth muscle contraction in the intestinal wall.

core.definition: The quality of acting or happening naturally and without planning, from impulse rather than deliberate design.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'NEE', and the 'ee' before 'ah' is a glide. The last syllable is a reduced 'tee', so avoid stressing the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests freshness, energy and freedom from rigid planning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'spontaneity' to praise an unplanned, lively quality, as in a trip or a conversation. In business it may describe a team culture of flexibility. It is a bit more formal than 'spontaneous' and sounds natural in writing or serious talk.

distinctions.note: 'Impulsiveness' often suggests acting without thinking, which may be negative, while 'spontaneity' is usually positive.
'Improvisation' is making something up on the spot, usually in art or performance, while 'spontaneity' is the general quality.

examples.everyday: I love the spontaneity of a road trip with no set plan.
examples.professional: The team kept some spontaneity in meetings, which led to better ideas.
examples.analytical: Her theology stresses the spontaneity of grace, which cannot be earned or planned.

nuance.analogy: Spontaneity is like a river that finds its own way down the hill rather than following a pipe.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin 'spontaneus', from 'sponte', of one's own accord.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable instead of 'NEE'.
Using 'spontaneity' when 'spontaneousness' is more natural in some formal contexts.

senses.definition: A miscarriage.

core.definition: The medical term for a miscarriage: the natural loss of a pregnancy before the fetus can survive outside the womb.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TAY in 'spontaneous' and BOR in 'abortion'. The vowels in both words are reduced, and the final '-tion' is pronounced 'shun', not 'shin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical, but it can sound cold or confusing to a patient who has lost a pregnancy.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say miscarriage. Spontaneous abortion is used mainly by doctors, nurses and in medical writing. Because abortion in American English usually means a deliberate, induced termination, this term can cause confusion or distress, so use miscarriage when speaking to friends or patients.

distinctions.note: Miscarriage is the everyday American term for the same event; spontaneous abortion is the clinical term used in medical records and research.
Stillbirth is the death of a baby after about 20 weeks of pregnancy, while a spontaneous abortion occurs earlier.
Induced abortion is a deliberate ending of a pregnancy; spontaneous abortion happens naturally without intervention.

collocations: a spontaneous abortion in the first trimester

examples.everyday: The nurse explained that a spontaneous abortion is the medical term for a miscarriage.
examples.professional: The clinical notes list two prior spontaneous abortions, so the team ordered genetic testing.
examples.analytical: Ethicists note that the phrase spontaneous abortion carries an uneasy tension, since abortion usually refers to a deliberate choice.

nuance.analogy: It is like a formal label on a file: accurate in a medical chart, but unfamiliar and jarring in ordinary conversation.
nuance.etymology: Spontaneous from Latin spontaneus, of one's own accord; abortion from Latin abortio, the premature ending of a pregnancy.
common_mistakes: Using spontaneous abortion casually with friends; miscarriage is the natural everyday word.
Pronouncing abortion with a stressed final syllable, as in 'uh-bor-SHUN'.

senses.definition: In the shape of a square; at right angles.
senses.example: She folded the napkin squarely into a perfect square before setting the table.

senses.definition: Firmly and solidly.
In a direct, straightforward and honest manner.

core.definition: Directly and firmly, right on the target or exactly where it belongs, with full responsibility.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SKWAIR. The final -ly is a weak 'lee' sound, so do not stress it or make the middle sound like 'squirl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strong. It often assigns responsibility, so it can sound blaming or affirming depending on the context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use squarely in news, political writing, and formal speech, as in 'the blame falls squarely on management.' In casual talk, people also say 'that's squarely my fault' to take responsibility. It usually comes before a preposition such as on, in, or behind.

distinctions.note: Directly means without going through anything else, while squarely adds a sense of full, firm placement or responsibility.
Straight means without deviation, while squarely emphasizes that something lands fully on a specific target or person.
Frankly means honestly and openly in speech, while squarely describes firm placement of responsibility or position.

examples.everyday: I didn't close the gate, so honestly the mess is squarely my fault, and I'll clean it up.
examples.professional: The delay falls squarely on the vendor, so we should escalate it with their account team this afternoon.
examples.analytical: The argument rests squarely on the premise that moral obligations can be discovered by reason alone.

nuance.analogy: It is like hitting the bullseye: the arrow lands squarely in the center rather than off to one side.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective square, plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the second syllable, as in 'skwair-LEE', which makes the word sound unnatural.
Using squarely informally in place of right in the middle, as in 'squarely in the room'; 'right in the middle' is more natural in casual speech.

senses.definition: A complainer; one who speaks out when there are problems.
senses.example: In our office, the squeaky wheel always gets the attention, so complaining works.

senses.definition: Of several problems, the most apparent or the most urgent.
senses.example: Staffing shortages were the squeaky wheel, and fixing them became our top priority.

core.definition: A person who complains loudly and persistently, so that they get attention and help.

pronunciation.tip: Put secondary stress on the first word and primary stress on wheel. The -y in squeaky is a long EE, and wheel is one syllable with a long EE too.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It can praise persistence or criticize someone who complains too much, depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the squeaky wheel gets the grease' to mean that people who complain get noticed and helped. Use it casually at work or at home. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I guess I need to speak up,' or simply a laugh. Said about a person, it may sound mildly critical.

distinctions.note: Complainer is plainly negative; squeaky wheel can suggest that the complaint is justified and effective.
