common_mistakes: Adding a vowel and saying 'sur-ge' instead of one syllable ending in the soft j sound.
Using surge for slow, steady growth; Americans would say 'a gradual increase' or 'steady growth' instead.
Writing 'a surge of' followed by a number of percent without context, which sounds vague; say 'a surge in' plus the thing that rose.
nuance.biblical_note: Surge is not a key biblical term. In the Revised Standard Version, Jeremiah 46:7-8 uses the image of rivers whose waters surge, to describe the rising force of an army like the Nile in flood.

surge.etymology: The verb is from Middle English, possibly from Middle French *sourgir*, from Old French *surgir* (“to rise, ride near the shore, arrive, land”), from *surgir*, from Latin *surgō*, contraction of *surrigō*, *subrigō* (“lift up, raise, erect; intransitive…

senses.definition: A person occupied with surveying: the process of determining positions on the earth's surface.
senses.example: The surveyor set up her transit on the hill to mark the property boundary.

senses.definition: One who carries out a survey or poll.
senses.example: The surveyor knocked on doors all afternoon, collecting answers for the city's housing study.

core.definition: A professional who measures and maps land, property boundaries, and elevations to determine exact positions and dimensions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, VAY, while the first and last syllables are weak. Many learners stress the first syllable, as in 'SUR-vey-or', which sounds unnatural.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it describes a respected, licensed professional whose measurements matter legally and financially.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say land surveyor when talking about the job, especially when buying property or planning construction. In casual speech people may just say surveyor or the survey crew. A surveyor measures land, while an inspector checks a building for code compliance and condition.

distinctions.note: An inspector checks whether a building or product meets codes or standards, while a surveyor measures land and locates boundaries or elevations.
An appraiser estimates the value of property, while a surveyor measures its physical boundaries and features.
A pollster conducts opinion polls, which use the same root survey in a different sense, while a surveyor measures land.

examples.everyday: The surveyor came out last week to mark the property line before we put up the fence.
examples.professional: The civil engineering team needs the surveyor's elevation data before it can finalize the drainage plan.
examples.analytical: A surveyor's map is only as reliable as the reference points on which every measurement depends.

nuance.analogy: A surveyor is like a careful carpenter working from a chalk line: every later measurement depends on that first accurate mark.
nuance.etymology: From survey, from Anglo-French surveier, 'to look over,' with the agent suffix -or.
common_mistakes: Using the spelling or pronunciation 'surveyer', which is not standard.
Confusing a surveyor with an inspector or appraiser, since all three evaluate property in different ways.

surveyor.etymology: From Middle English *surveyour*, from Anglo-Norman *surveour*, from Old French *sorveor*.

senses.definition: One who or that which operates a switch.
senses.example: The night switcher at the telephone exchange connected every call by hand.

senses.definition: One who or that which switches, that is, changes in some way.
senses.example: career switcher

senses.definition: A switchmode power supply.
senses.example: Our new laptop charger uses a switcher that keeps the output steady and efficient.

senses.definition: A railway locomotive used for shunting (switching).
senses.example: The switcher pushed the boxcars onto the siding before the freight train left.

senses.definition: The yardman who operates such an engine, or performs a similar role in a trucking depot.
senses.example: The switcher waved the truck into bay four without even looking at the manifest.

senses.definition: Synonym of vision mixer (“device for selecting between video sources”).
senses.example: During the live broadcast, the switcher cut between the four camera feeds smoothly.

core.definition: A person or device that switches between options or inputs, such as a brand switcher or a video switcher.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SWITCH, and end with a light American r in the reduced final syllable. Don't pronounce the ch as a separate t and sh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is descriptive, and a 'switcher' is often a neutral or slightly negative label in marketing contexts.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American talk, people use switcher for consumers who change brands, jobs or service providers, as in 'brand switcher'. In technical settings, a video switcher selects among cameras, and a KVM switcher selects among computers. Don't use it for a light switch; that is simply a switch.

distinctions.note: A switch is the physical part or the action; a switcher is the person or device that performs switching.
A converter changes a signal or format into another; a switcher selects among inputs without changing them.

examples.everyday: I'm a brand switcher, so I just buy whatever cereal is on sale.
examples.professional: The video switcher lets us cut between the two cameras during the live stream.
examples.analytical: Economists divide consumers into loyal buyers and switchers, a distinction that shapes how firms price long-term relationships.

nuance.analogy: A switcher is like a railroad switchman who decides which track the train takes.
nuance.etymology: Formed from switch with the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using switcher for a light switch; the correct term is switch.
Confusing switcher with converter when the device selects inputs rather than changing their format.

senses.definition: A compilation of hagiographies in the Eastern Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Eastern Catholic Churches, corresponding roughly to the martyrology of the Roman Church.

core.definition: A collection of short saints' lives arranged by calendar day, read in Eastern Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, SAIR, in American speech. Pronounce the x as a k plus s sound, and reduce the final syllables to un. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the x like a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized religious term that describes a book or reading without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use synaxarion mainly in Orthodox parishes, seminaries, monasteries and academic writing about church history. In a general conversation a person might say 'the book of saints' or 'the Orthodox calendar of saints' instead. Its Roman Catholic counterpart is the martyrology, which Americans sometimes compare to it.

distinctions.note: A martyrology is the Roman Catholic daily list of martyrs and saints, usually brief and formal; a synaxarion is an Eastern collection with fuller narratives read in the liturgy.
Hagiography is the general word for writing about saints' lives, while synaxarion refers to a specific calendar-based collection.
A Menaion is a liturgical book of fixed feasts for each month, and it often includes synaxarion entries for those days.

examples.everyday: At the monastery, a monk reads the synaxarion aloud before breakfast, so we hear about one saint each day.
examples.professional: Our parish library has a Greek synaxarion, and we use its entries for the weekly bulletin notes.
examples.analytical: The synaxarion's entries reveal how the Byzantine church shaped memory of martyrs through short, liturgically read narratives.

nuance.analogy: Like a daily devotional calendar that tells a short story about a saint for each date.
nuance.etymology: From Greek sunaxarion, a collection of saints' lives read on a given day, from sunaxis, 'assembly,' from sunagein, 'to bring together.'
common_mistakes: Confusing synaxarion with synaxis, which refers to a liturgical gathering rather than a book.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the third (sair) in American speech.

synaxarion.etymology: From Ancient Greek *συναξάριον*, from *συνάγειν* (“to bring together”).

senses.definition: Any thick liquid that has a high sugar content and which is added to or poured over food as a flavoring.
senses.example: maple syrup

senses.definition: Any viscous liquid.
senses.example: cough syrup

senses.definition: Anything overly sweet or sentimental.
senses.example: His speech was pure syrup, full of cheap compliments and sugary sentimental clichés.

senses.definition: To convert or process into syrup.
senses.example: Each spring the family syrups the maple sap in a small shed out back.

senses.definition: To add syrup to.
senses.example: Grandma always syrups her pancakes with real maple syrup from Vermont.

senses.definition: To sabotage (a vehicle) by pouring syrup into the gas tank.
senses.example: Rival mechanics syruped the truck's gas tank overnight to ruin its engine.

core.definition: A thick, sweet liquid made by dissolving sugar in water, used to flavor foods like pancakes, desserts, and drinks.

pronunciation.tip: The first vowel is a short 'i' like in 'sit', and the r is pronounced clearly, so it is 'SIR-up' rather than 'SEER-up' or 'SIGH-rup'. The second syllable is an unstressed 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a pleasant everyday word, though it can sound negative when describing something too sweet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'syrup' constantly, especially for maple syrup on pancakes and for corn syrup in processed foods. The word also covers liquid cough medicine, so 'cough syrup' is a common phrase. Americans do not usually say 'sirup', which is an older or British-influenced spelling.

distinctions.note: Molasses is much thicker and darker, made when sugar is refined, while syrup is a lighter, sweeter liquid.
Jam is a thick fruit spread with chunks of fruit, while syrup is a smooth liquid poured over food.

examples.everyday: Can you pass the maple syrup? These pancakes are a little dry.
examples.professional: We need to lower the cost of corn syrup in the beverage formula before the next quarter.
examples.analytical: The sweetness of the dessert depends on the syrup's sugar concentration more than on its flavor.

nuance.analogy: Syrup is like honey that has been thinned with water and sugar, a liquid that flows slowly and clings to whatever you pour it on.
nuance.etymology: From Old French sirop, from Medieval Latin siropus, from Arabic sharab, 'a drink.'
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'sirup', which is outdated in American English.
Pronouncing it 'SY-rup' with a long i, which is a common mistake.
Using 'syrup' for jam or jelly, which are thicker and contain fruit pieces.

syrup.etymology: From Middle English *sirup*, from Old French *sirop*, from Medieval Latin *siruppus*, *syrupus*, from Arabic *شَرَاب* (“a drink, beverage, wine, coffee, syrup”), from *شَرِبَ* (“to drink”).

senses.definition: A mind, as of a newborn, free of any impressions, notions, ideas, etc.
Anything which exists in a pristine state.
senses.example: Her first semester at the new school felt like a tabula rasa, with no reputation to defend.

core.definition: In philosophy, a mind imagined as blank at birth, free of ideas before experience. In everyday use, anything in a fresh, unmarked state.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have primary stress on their first syllable, TAB and RAY, with the second syllable weak. Americans usually say the Latin phrase in English style, not with Latin vowels. Pronounce 'rasa' as 'RAY-zuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; it can also be used playfully for a fresh start.
nuance.usage_note: Philosophy courses in the US use this phrase when discussing John Locke. In casual speech Americans prefer 'clean slate' or 'fresh start' for the same idea. Using 'tabula rasa' in conversation can sound academic, so use it with care.

distinctions.note: Clean slate is the everyday American equivalent for a fresh start; tabula rasa is more philosophical or academic.
Innate refers to ideas present from birth; tabula rasa is the opposite claim that the mind starts empty.

collocations: tabula rasa view of the mind
approach a problem as tabula rasa

examples.everyday: After that rough year, I'm going in with a tabula rasa, so let's start fresh.
examples.professional: For the redesign, let's approach the legacy system as a tabula rasa rather than patching old code.
examples.analytical: Locke's image of the mind as tabula rasa challenged the rationalist claim that some ideas are innate.

nuance.analogy: Like a whiteboard that has been completely wiped clean and is ready for new writing.
nuance.etymology: Latin, meaning 'scraped tablet', a wax writing tablet cleared of its marks.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the Latin vowels in a classical way rather than the English way.
Using it casually in ordinary speech where 'clean slate' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with the idea of innate knowledge, which is the opposite view.

tabula-rasa.etymology: where the collocation comprised *tabula* (“wax-covered writing tablet”) + *rāsa*, feminine singular of *rāsus* (“scraped, erased, cleaned”).

senses.definition: To assert an opinion or viewpoint; to defend one's point of view or beliefs.
senses.example: There will come a time when you'll need to take a stand for the changes you want.

core.definition: To state a clear position on an issue and defend it publicly, especially on a matter of principle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'stand', with a short vowel like 'hand', not 'stund'. Link 'take a' smoothly and keep the final d crisp.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests courage and conviction, though it can sound stubborn if the issue is trivial.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this for serious matters in politics, ethics, and the workplace, as in 'The school took a stand against bullying.' It sounds weighty, so save it for real principles rather than small preferences. A natural reply is 'I respect that' or 'Good for them.'

distinctions.note: 'Take a position' is more neutral and often used in formal, analytical writing, while 'take a stand' carries more moral force.
'Stand up for' means to defend a specific person or value, while 'take a stand' means to state a public position on an issue.
'Make a stand' emphasizes resisting firmly, often under pressure, while 'take a stand' can be a calm, public declaration.

examples.everyday: My neighbor finally took a stand against the loud construction next door and called the city.
examples.professional: Legal took a stand that we can't publish the data without consent, and I agree with them.
examples.analytical: A philosopher who takes a stand on free will must explain how moral responsibility survives determinism.

nuance.analogy: Like planting a flag on a piece of ground and refusing to move it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'take stand' without the article 'a'.
Using 'take a stand for' loosely; Americans more often say 'take a stand on' or 'take a stand against'.

senses.definition: Referring to a tangent, moving at a tangent to something.
senses.example: The velocity vector is tangential to the curve at every point along its path.

senses.definition: Merely touching, positioned as a tangent.
senses.example: The two roads share only a tangential connection, meeting briefly at one small intersection.

senses.definition: Only indirectly related.
senses.example: That subject is tangential to our discussion, and we cannot let it distract us.

core.definition: Only slightly or indirectly related to the main topic, or in geometry, touching a curve at a single point.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'JEN'. The 'tial' ending is pronounced 'shul', not 'tee-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative in conversation, because it often suggests a point that does not matter much to the discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tangential in academic writing, meetings, and technical discussions to say a point is not central. In casual speech, people more often say 'off-topic' or 'not really related'. It is a precise but somewhat formal word.

distinctions.note: Peripheral means on the outer edge of something, while tangential means related only slightly in topic or in geometry.
Irrelevant means not related at all, while tangential suggests a weak but real connection.

examples.everyday: That story about my old job was kind of tangential, so I'll get back to your question.
examples.professional: Your point about the logo is tangential to our data quality problem, so let's park it for the next meeting.
examples.analytical: The author treats the economic claims as tangential to the theological argument, which weakens the case for their importance.

nuance.analogy: A tangential comment is like a car that brushes past the main road at a single point and then leaves.
nuance.etymology: From tangent, from Latin tangere, meaning 'to touch'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'TAN-jen-shul'.
Using tangential to mean 'tangent' as a noun.

senses.definition: A piece of work done as part of one’s duties.
senses.example: daily task, monotonous task, regular task, parental task

senses.definition: A state of diligence in work on a task.
senses.example: I put him to task on the chores.

senses.definition: Any piece of work done.
senses.example: carry out a task

senses.definition: A single action undertaken by a given agent.
senses.example: Each member of the team completed tasks in service of the goal.

senses.definition: A difficult or tedious undertaking; a substantial project.
senses.example: Getting him to change his behavior will be quite a task for you.

senses.definition: An objective or duty.
senses.example: Your task is the elimination of the termites.

senses.definition: A process or execution of a program.
senses.example: The user killed the frozen task.

senses.definition: State of being subject to reprimands.
senses.example: call to task, take to task

senses.definition: To assign a task to; to impose a task on.
senses.example: On my first day in the office, I was tasked with sorting a pile of invoices.

senses.definition: To oppress with severe or excessive burdens; to tax.
senses.example: Endless paperwork tasks small clinics, leaving nurses too exhausted to care for patients.

senses.definition: To charge, as with a fault.
senses.example: The old pastor tasked the young deacon with neglecting his duties.

core.definition: A specific piece of work someone is assigned to do, especially as part of a job or a larger project.

pronunciation.tip: The word is one syllable with a short a. Keep the final sk cluster crisp and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound burdensome when the work is difficult or unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use task for a defined piece of work, especially in offices, software projects, and military or government contexts. In casual talk people more often say job, chore, or thing to do, and task can sound a little formal. The word is common in project management, where a task is a small unit within a larger project.

distinctions.note: A chore is a routine, often dull household or farm job; a task can be any defined piece of work, including a challenging professional one.
A job can mean a whole paid position or a complete piece of work, while a task is a smaller unit within it.
A duty is a moral or official obligation; a task is a specific activity you carry out, regardless of obligation.

examples.everyday: Could you do one small task for me and grab some milk on your way home?
examples.professional: Please assign the data cleaning task to Priya before Friday's sprint review.
examples.analytical: Kant treats the moral task as one that no finite agent completes, only continually approaches.

nuance.analogy: A single stitch in a larger quilt: each task is small on its own, but the whole project depends on it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French tasche, from Medieval Latin tasca, meaning tax.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tasked to do' where the natural phrase is 'tasked with doing' or 'tasked with a task'.
Using task for a whole career or project; a job or project is the broader term.

task.etymology: From Middle English *taske* (“task, tax”), from *tasque*, (compare Old French variant *tasche*), from Medieval Latin *tasca*, alteration of *taxa*, from Latin *taxō* (“to censure; to charge”).

senses.definition: In a tasteful manner.

core.definition: In a way that shows good judgment about style, appropriateness or quality, without being excessive or vulgar.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The -ful is unstressed and reduces to a short fuh, and the final -ly is a clear ee sound, not lie.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises restraint, good judgment and appropriateness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tastefully for decor, clothing, speech or jokes that are appropriate. It is a compliment for a restrained approach, and it often appears in phrases like tastefully decorated or tastefully done. It is common in real estate listings, reviews and everyday praise.

distinctions.note: Elegantly stresses grace and polish; tastefully stresses restraint and appropriateness, so it is less about being fancy.
Classy is informal and can sound like praise of wealth; tastefully focuses on sensible judgment.
Subtly means in a delicate, hard-to-notice way; tastefully means appropriately, with good judgment.

examples.everyday: Their living room is tastefully decorated, with plants and a few nice paintings.
examples.professional: Please handle the layoff announcement tastefully and keep the message short and respectful.
examples.analytical: Her memoir treats grief tastefully, avoiding both sensationalism and false cheer.

nuance.analogy: Being tastefully done is like a well-tailored suit: nothing flashy, and everything fits the occasion.
nuance.etymology: From tasteful, from taste (judgment) plus -ful, with the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -ful syllable, as in taste-FUL-ly.
Confusing tastefully with tastily, which means in a tasty way.

senses.definition: Having force, or having a marked effect; weighty, effective.
senses.example: a telling blow

senses.definition: Revealing information; bearing significance.
senses.example: a telling smile

senses.definition: Serving to convince.
senses.example: telling evidence

senses.definition: The act of narration.
senses.example: The telling of the story took nearly an hour, with long pauses for dramatic effect.

senses.definition: The disclosure of information.
senses.example: Her telling of the secret to reporters cost her the job she loved.

senses.definition: Ability to determine.
senses.example: Her telling of counterfeit bills was so sharp that the cashier never got fooled.

core.definition: Having a clear, significant effect; revealing what is really true about a situation or what someone really thinks or feels.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The vowel in the first syllable is short, as in 'tell', not 'tail', and the ending is a short 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it describes something that clearly reveals or matters; it can be negative if the revealed thing is bad, as in a telling sign of trouble.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'telling' most often in phrases like 'a telling detail' or 'a telling sign', meaning something that shows what is really going on. It is common in conversation, writing and the news, and it is not stiff or formal. Do not confuse the adjective with the verb 'tell'.

distinctions.note: 'Revealing' often describes clothing or an accidental disclosure, while 'telling' means a fact or detail that clearly shows something important about a situation or character.
'Significant' means important in general; 'telling' stresses that something exposes the true nature of a situation.

examples.everyday: Her hesitation before answering was a telling sign that she didn't want to go.
examples.professional: The drop in repeat customers is a telling statistic, so we should look at why people stop using the app.
examples.analytical: Her silence during the debate was more telling than any argument she could have made.

nuance.analogy: Like a fever reading that reveals illness before the patient says anything, a telling detail shows what is happening underneath.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'tell', from Old English tellan, 'to count, reckon, relate'; the adjective is a participial form.
common_mistakes: Using 'tell' as an adjective: say 'a telling sign', not 'a tell sign'.
Using the adjective as a verb: say 'She told me', not 'She telling me'.

senses.definition: The state of being thankful.

core.definition: The quality or state of feeling and showing gratitude.

pronunciation.tip: Stress THANK. The nk is one nasal sound, the middle syllable is reduced to fuhl, and the final -ness has a short e.

nuance.connotation: Positive and sincere. It sounds warmer and more personal than 'gratitude' in many contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thankfulness in church, sermons, prayers and personal reflection. In everyday talk, 'gratitude' is more common. For the holiday, Americans say Thanksgiving, not thankfulness. The word works well in toasts or letters.

distinctions.note: Gratitude is the more general and modern word, often used in psychology and everyday speech, while thankfulness sounds more personal and warm.
Thanksgiving is the act of giving thanks, especially to God, or the American holiday.

examples.everyday: There was real thankfulness in her voice when she saw her son walk through the door.
examples.professional: Let's open the meeting with a moment of thankfulness for the team's work this quarter.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters often move from thankfulness to instruction, suggesting that gratitude shapes the believer's ethical life.

nuance.analogy: It is like a bank account of blessings: the more deposits you notice, the richer you feel.
nuance.etymology: From thankful plus the suffix -ness; the root is Old English thanc, 'thought, gratitude'.
common_mistakes: Confusing thankfulness with thanksgiving, which is the holiday or the act of thanks.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on THANK.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, todah (תּוֹדָה) means thanksgiving or a thanksgiving offering, and the Greek word eucharistia means giving thanks. Key passages are 1 Thessalonians 5:18, which calls believers to give thanks in all circumstances, Colossians 3:15, which tells believers to be thankful, and Psalm 100:4, which invites worshipers to enter God's gates with thanksgiving.

senses.definition: Relatively great in extent from one surface to the opposite in its smallest solid dimension.
Measuring a certain number of units in this dimension.
senses.example: I want some planks that are two inches thick.

senses.definition: Heavy in build; thickset.
senses.example: He had such a thick neck that he had to turn his body to look to the side.

senses.definition: Densely crowded or packed.
senses.example: We walked through thick undergrowth.

senses.definition: Having a viscous consistency.
senses.example: My mum’s gravy was thick but at least it moved about.

senses.definition: Abounding in number.
senses.example: The room was thick with reporters.

senses.definition: Impenetrable to sight.
senses.example: We drove through thick fog.

senses.definition: (Of an accent) Prominent, strong.
senses.example: He answered me in his characteristically thick Creole patois.

senses.definition: Greatly evocative of one's nationality or place of origin.
senses.example: He answered me in his characteristically thick Creole patois.

senses.definition: Difficult to understand, or poorly articulated.
senses.example: We had difficulty understanding him with his thick accent.

senses.definition: Stupid.
senses.example: He was as thick as two short planks.

senses.definition: Friendly or intimate.
senses.example: They were as thick as thieves.

senses.definition: Deep, intense, or profound.
senses.example: Thick darkness.

senses.definition: Detailed and expansive; substantive.
Troublesome; unreasonable.
Curvy and voluptuous, and especially having large hips.
In a thick manner.
senses.example: Snow lay thick on the ground.

senses.definition: Frequently or numerously.
senses.example: The arrows flew thick and fast around us.

senses.definition: The thickest, or most active or intense, part of something.
senses.example: It was mayhem in the thick of battle.

senses.definition: A thicket.
A stupid person; a fool.

core.definition: Having a large distance between two opposite surfaces; not thin. Also used for liquids that are dense and flow slowly.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, as in 'sit,' not a long 'ee.' Keep the final k crisp and unvoiced, and avoid adding a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing objects, food, or liquids. Negative when used for people, as in 'thick' meaning stupid, which is rude and informal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thick' constantly for food and objects: a thick steak, thick bread, a thick sweater. Describing a person as 'thick' to mean stupid is informal and can offend, so use it only with close friends, if at all. For a heavy build, Americans prefer 'stocky' or 'heavyset'; 'thickset' sounds literary.

distinctions.note: 'Thick' refers to the smallest dimension of a solid, such as a board's depth; 'wide' refers to side-to-side extent.
'Thick' is everyday and describes how much something fills space in one dimension; 'dense' is more technical or scientific and refers to mass or concentration per unit of volume.
'Thick' as an insult is informal and mild, while 'stupid' is blunter and more hurtful.

examples.everyday: This soup is too thick, so I'm going to add a little more broth.
examples.professional: The concrete slab needs to be six inches thick, so please check the forms before the crew pours tomorrow.
examples.analytical: A thick description, in Clifford Geertz's sense, records the context that makes a behavior meaningful rather than merely listing what people did.

nuance.analogy: Think of a thick book versus a thin pamphlet: thickness is how far it reaches from the front cover to the back.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'thicce,' meaning dense or close together.
common_mistakes: Saying 'thick' for a person's body size in polite speech; say 'heavyset' or 'stocky' instead.
Pronouncing it with a long vowel, as 'theek.'

thick.etymology: From Middle English *thikke*, from Old English *þicce* (“thick, dense”), from **þikkwī*, from Proto-Germanic **þekuz* (“thick”), from Proto-Indo-European **tégus* (“thick”).

senses.definition: A rack of thirty beers.
senses.example: She grabbed a thirty of beer from the cooler for the barbecue.

senses.definition: A commercial lasting 30 seconds.
senses.example: The company's new thirty ran during the Super Bowl and sparked a lot of online debate.

core.definition: The cardinal number 30, equal to three tens; also used for the age range or years from thirty to thirty-nine, as in 'in my thirties'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, unlike 'thirteen', which is stressed on the second. In fast speech the t may sound like a soft d, as in 'THUR-dee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'thirty' all the time for numbers, prices, ages, and time, such as 'thirty minutes' or 'a thirty-year mortgage'. For ages, Americans often say 'in my thirties' or 'mid-thirties'. In journalism, '-30-' has traditionally marked the end of a story, but this is now rare outside newsrooms.

distinctions.note: 'Thirty' has stress on the first syllable, while 'thirteen' has stress on the second; the difference is important in conversation about numbers.
'Thirty' is the cardinal number, used for counting, while 'thirtieth' is the ordinal, used for position, such as the thirtieth floor.

examples.everyday: The store is only thirty minutes away, so we can still make the movie.
examples.professional: We expect about thirty percent of users to switch to the new dashboard in the first month.
examples.analytical: The sample of thirty participants is small, so the confidence intervals are necessarily wide.

nuance.analogy: Like three stacks of ten coins, thirty is simply three tens put together.
nuance.etymology: From Old English thritig, meaning three tens, from 'three' plus the suffix '-ty' for tens.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'thirty' and 'thirteen' in speech; practice the stress on the first syllable of 'thirty' and the second of 'thirteen'.
Saying 'in the thirty' for an age range; the correct phrase is 'in my thirties'.

thirty.etymology: From Middle English *thirty*, metathetic alternant of *thritty*, from Old English *þrītiġ*, *þrittiġ* (“thirty”), from Proto-Germanic **þrīz tigiwiz* (“thirty”), equivalent to *three* + *-ty*.

senses.definition: Synonym of timesheet.
A note provided by a contractor indicating the number of hours for which a worker is due to be paid.
senses.example: The contractor attached a time check showing forty hours for the electrician's week.

senses.definition: An instance of checking the amount of time required to cover a specific distance, occurring at a prearranged point in a race.
senses.example: At the five-kilometer mark, the time check showed she was ahead of schedule.

core.definition: A record of the hours a worker has put in, used to calculate how much pay they are owed.

pronunciation.tip: As a compound noun, 'time check' usually puts the main stress on TIME, with a lighter stress on check. Do not stress both words equally, and keep the ch sound crisp, as in 'church'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a practical, administrative term.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, people more often say timesheet or time sheet for the record of hours worked. Time check appears in some payroll, contracting and sports timing contexts. In a meeting, use timesheet unless your company uses the term, and then follow its usage.

distinctions.note: Timesheet is the standard American term for the hours record; time check is less common and mainly used in certain contracting or payroll settings.

examples.everyday: My neighbor, who does drywall, says he has to send his time check to the office every Friday.
examples.professional: Please submit your time check by noon Friday so payroll can process the contractor invoices.
examples.analytical: A time check functions as a verifiable record of labor, which is why auditors examine it when disputes about billed hours arise.

nuance.analogy: A time check is like a bank statement for your hours: it shows what was logged so the paycheck can be calculated.
nuance.etymology: Compound of time (from Old English tima) and check (from Old French eschec, a term from chess).
common_mistakes: Using time check when Americans would normally say timesheet or time sheet.
Stressing both words equally, instead of putting primary stress on TIME.

conversation.text: Quick time check: we have ten minutes left.
Time check, everyone. We still have three items on the agenda.
Can I get a time check? I have another call at eleven.

senses.definition: A mine from which tin is extracted.

core.definition: A mine from which tin ore is dug out of the ground, usually an underground or open-pit site.

pronunciation.tip: In compounds like this, American speech puts the main stress on the first word, TIN mine, as in coal mine, so the given stress pattern is corrected. Say mine with a clear long i, like 'mine' in 'mind'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; it is a factual term without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tin mine mostly in history, geology, economics and news about mining in countries such as Bolivia or Malaysia. In everyday talk, people usually just say mine or mining. The word is clear and widely understood.

distinctions.note: Mine is the general term for an excavation that extracts minerals; tin mine specifies the metal being extracted.
A tin works is a plant that smelts or processes tin ore, while a tin mine is where the ore is dug out.

examples.everyday: We drove past an old tin mine on the way to the lake, and my kids asked a hundred questions about it.
examples.professional: The supplier's tin mine in Bolivia has delayed shipments, so we may need a second source before next quarter.
examples.analytical: The economic history of colonial Bolivia is hard to separate from the silver and tin mines that shaped its labor system.

nuance.analogy: A tin mine is like a cupboard where the metal is stored inside rock until someone digs it out.
nuance.etymology: Tin is from Old English tin; mine is from Old French mine, of uncertain Celtic origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing mine as the main word, as in tin MINE; the first word normally takes the main stress.
Confusing a tin mine with a tin works, which processes the ore rather than extracting it.

senses.definition: A person who tolls a bell; a bell ringer.
A person who collects tolls; a tollkeeper.
senses.example: The toller at the old bridge waved us through after taking our coins for the crossing.

senses.definition: Clipping of Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever.
senses.example: Our family adopted a toller puppy, and she loves fetching tennis balls from the lake.

core.definition: A person who rings a bell slowly and steadily, especially a church bell, to mark a death or service.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so the ending sounds like 'ler', not 'lor' or 'tail-er'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, somewhat old-fashioned word for a specific job.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use toller for a bell ringer and would more likely say bell ringer or someone who rings the bell. In dog circles, toller is a short name for the Nova Scotia Duck Tolling Retriever, a breed known for luring ducks. Outside dog fancy, most people will not know the bell sense, so explain it if you use it.

distinctions.note: Bell ringer is the common American term, while toller is rarer and more literary.
A toll-taker collects fees on a road, while a toller rings a bell; the words share a root but not a meaning.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's toller at the old church still rings the bell every Sunday morning.
examples.professional: The parish needs a volunteer toller for funeral services, so please let the office know if you can help.
examples.analytical: In the medieval village, the toller marked the hours and deaths, binding the community through sound.

nuance.analogy: Like a metronome in a church tower, keeping steady time for the whole town.
nuance.etymology: From toll, to ring a bell slowly, from Middle English tollen, to pull or draw.
common_mistakes: Confusing toller with tolerate or with taller, since the words sound similar.
Using toller for a toll collector; that person is a toll-taker.

senses.definition: Lots; large quantities or numbers (of people or things).
senses.example: I have tons of pens, but none of them work.

core.definition: A very large amount or number of something; lots of people, things or time.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short uh vowel of cup and end with a clean z. Keep the t crisp; it is at the start of the word, so it is not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It is enthusiastic and casual.
nuance.usage_note: 'Tons of' is casual American speech: 'I have tons of work' or 'There's tons of parking.' It is used in conversation, not formal writing, and needs a plural or uncountable noun after it. In formal writing, say 'large quantities' or 'many'.

distinctions.note: Both are informal and nearly interchangeable; tons of sounds more emphatic.
A ton is a unit of weight, 2,000 pounds in the US; informally, a ton means a large amount.

examples.everyday: We had tons of fun at the lake this weekend.
examples.professional: There are tons of edge cases to test before the release goes out.
examples.analytical: The dataset contains tons of noise, which makes it hard to isolate the signal.

nuance.analogy: Tons is a big pile that looks overwhelming from the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tunne, 'large cask', later used as a unit of weight.
common_mistakes: Writing 'a tons of'; say 'tons of' with no article.
Using tons in formal writing, where it sounds too casual; say 'large quantities' instead.

senses.definition: Having teeth.
senses.example: The sperm whale is a toothed whale.

senses.definition: Having projections resembling an animal's teeth.
senses.example: A cog is a toothed wheel.

senses.definition: Having teeth of the specified type.
senses.example: A sharp-toothed rat.

core.definition: Having teeth, or having sharp projections that work like teeth. Often used for saws, combs, gears, and some animals.

pronunciation.tip: The word ends in a 'th' sound followed by a 't', so say the consonant cluster smoothly without adding a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'toothed' mostly in technical or descriptive language, such as 'fine-toothed comb' or 'toothed belt' in machines. In everyday talk, people more often say 'with teeth' or 'with sharp edges.' Do not confuse it with 'toothy,' which describes a wide smile.

distinctions.note: 'Toothy' describes a big grin that shows many teeth, while 'toothed' describes the physical presence of teeth or projections.
'Serrated' is a technical term for a saw-like edge, while 'toothed' is broader and more general.

examples.everyday: Use the wide-toothed comb on the dog's knots so you don't pull the fur.
examples.professional: We need a toothed belt for the timing drive, because a smooth belt would slip under this load.
examples.analytical: Toothed whales are distinguished from baleen whales by their feeding anatomy, which shapes how they hunt.

nuance.analogy: A toothed edge is like a row of tiny hooks that catch and hold whatever moves against them.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'tooth' with the suffix '-ed', meaning having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'toothed' with 'toothy'; 'toothy' is about a big smile, while 'toothed' is about having teeth.
Adding an extra vowel in the pronunciation, making it 'tooth-ed' instead of one syllable.

senses.definition: A scientist or physician who specializes in toxicology.

core.definition: A scientist or physician who specializes in toxicology, the study of poisons and their effects on living things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the KAH syllable, and the -ol- of toxicology is pronounced like 'uh' in American speech, not like 'oh'. The final -ist is a reduced, quick syllable, like 'ist' in 'artist'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use toxicologist for a specialist who investigates poisons, drugs and chemical exposures, often in a hospital, a crime lab, a government agency or a university. In everyday talk people might say 'a poison expert' or 'a doctor who specializes in poisoning,' but toxicologist is the precise professional term. A clinical toxicologist is usually a physician, while a forensic toxicologist works on legal cases.

distinctions.note: A pharmacologist studies how drugs act in the body in general, including helpful effects, while a toxicologist focuses on harmful effects and poisoning.
An epidemiologist studies patterns of disease across populations, whereas a toxicologist studies the chemical causes of harm in individuals or environments.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a toxicologist at the county hospital, so she knows a lot about carbon monoxide.
examples.professional: The toxicologist confirmed that the lab results showed no sign of a lethal dose.
examples.analytical: A good toxicologist distinguishes between the dose that makes a substance toxic and the exposure that actually causes harm.

nuance.analogy: A toxicologist is like a detective for chemicals, tracing the harm back to the dose and the body that received it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from toxicology plus the suffix -ist, meaning one who practices or specializes in a field.
common_mistakes: Saying 'toxicologist' with the stress on the wrong syllable, such as 'TAHK-sih-kol-uh-jist.'
Confusing toxicologist with toxician or toxin specialist; the standard American term is toxicologist.

senses.definition: A situation in which road traffic accumulates until it is stationary or very slow.

core.definition: A situation in which road traffic builds up and moves very slowly or stops completely for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, TRAF, and keep 'jam' lighter but still clear. The t in 'traffic' is a soft flap, and the final vowel in 'jam' is the short 'a' of 'cat', not 'jahm'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes frustrating delay, though it is a neutral description of a situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'traffic jam' for congestion on highways, bridges and city streets, and it is very common in news and everyday speech. For a larger total standstill, people may say 'gridlock'. Saying 'We got stuck in a traffic jam' is a natural way to explain lateness.

distinctions.note: Gridlock describes a total standstill across a whole road network, while a traffic jam can be a local build-up that is slow but moving.
Congestion is a general or technical term for crowded traffic, while traffic jam is a concrete, everyday expression for a specific delay.

examples.everyday: We got caught in a traffic jam on the bridge, so we missed the first half of the movie.
examples.professional: A traffic jam at the loading dock delayed our shipments, so please update the delivery schedule.
examples.analytical: The traffic jam illustrates how small individual decisions to merge can aggregate into collective delay.

nuance.analogy: A traffic jam is like a crowded doorway: everyone wants to go through at once, so no one moves quickly.
nuance.etymology: Traffic comes from Italian traffico; jam, meaning a crowded mass, was first used in the seventeenth century.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a traffic jams' or using the plural for one jam; the noun is countable in the singular: 'a traffic jam'.
Using 'traffic jam' for a single slow car; it describes a larger build-up of many vehicles.

conversation.text: We sat in a traffic jam for an hour because of the construction.
Sorry I'm late; I got stuck in a traffic jam on the bridge.
A truck broke down in the left lane and caused a huge traffic jam.

senses.definition: The belief that human beings are made up of three distinct components: body or flesh, soul, and spirit.

core.definition: The theological view that a human being consists of three distinct parts: body, soul, and spirit.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KAH, the second syllable. Keep the middle syllables light, and end with a clear '-izm' sound. Americans often pronounce the first syllable as 'try' rather than 'trick.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a position in theology and is discussed respectfully by scholars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in theology, Bible study, and academic discussions of human nature. It is often contrasted with dichotomism, the view that humans have only two parts, body and soul. In church conversation people might say 'do you think we have a spirit separate from our soul?' rather than using the word.

distinctions.note: Dichotomism holds that a person has two parts, body and soul (with spirit understood as part of the soul), while trichotomism treats soul and spirit as distinct.
Monism holds that a person is a single unified substance, while trichotomism divides the person into three components.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group got into an argument about whether we have a soul and a spirit or just one, and that's when trichotomism came up.
examples.professional: In the seminar, the professor compared trichotomism with dichotomism and asked us to write a short response to both views.
examples.analytical: Advocates of trichotomism appeal to 1 Thessalonians 5:23 to argue that spirit and soul are distinguishable functions within the human person.

nuance.analogy: Trichotomism is like dividing a house into three rooms, the body, the soul, and the spirit, while dichotomism says the spirit is just a room inside the soul.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tricha (in three) and tomē (cutting), with the suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Confusing trichotomism with trichotomy, which is a mathematical or logical term about three-way division.
Using it as a general word for dividing anything into three parts.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses several words for the human person. The Hebrew nephesh often means life, self, or soul, and the Hebrew ruach and Greek pneuma mean spirit or breath, while the Greek psychē and sōma mean soul and body. Trichotomists cite 1 Thessalonians 5:23, which mentions spirit and soul and body. They also cite Hebrews 4:12, which speaks of the word of God piercing to the division of soul and spirit. Other readers say these verses describe the whole person in different aspects rather than separate parts.

traditions.view: Many Eastern Orthodox writers distinguish soul and spirit, with the spirit (pneuma) as the highest aspect of the human person, but the Church has not formally settled whether this is a strict trichotomy.
Catholic teaching holds that the rational soul is the one form of the body, so the human person has body and soul as its two essential principles, and trichotomism is generally rejected.
Most Reformed and Lutheran theologians hold dichotomism, though some Lutheran and Keil-Delitzsch scholars and many Pentecostal and Holiness writers have defended trichotomism.

senses.definition: A person who believes that human beings are made up of three distinct components: body, soul, and spirit.

core.definition: A person who holds that human beings consist of three distinct parts: body, soul, and spirit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, KOT, and reduce the 'tuh' in the middle. The 'o' in the stressed syllable is the American cot vowel, not 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a position in theology or philosophy and does not carry a positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term almost only in theology, church history, or philosophy of human nature, often in a seminary or academic setting. In a friendly discussion you might say, 'I'm a trichotomist, I think spirit is distinct from soul.' People in general conversation would not know the word, so explain it briefly when you use it.

distinctions.note: A dichotomist holds that humans have two parts, body and soul, while a trichotomist adds a separate spirit.
A monist holds that human beings are a single unified substance, which differs from both views about parts.

examples.everyday: At our Bible study, Jim is a trichotomist, so he always talks about body, soul, and spirit as separate.
examples.professional: For the seminary curriculum, we need to explain why some trichotomists read 1 Thessalonians 5:23 as describing three distinct parts.
examples.analytical: The trichotomist reads Paul's triad as a deliberate anthropological statement, while the dichotomist treats the spirit as the soul's higher dimension.

nuance.analogy: A trichotomist is like someone who sorts a house into three rooms, while a dichotomist sees only two.
nuance.etymology: From Greek trikha (threefold) and tomos (cutting), with the suffix -ist for a holder of a view.
common_mistakes: Confusing trichotomist with trichotomous, which is an adjective.
Stressing the first syllable as in 'TRY-ko-tom-ist'.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Greek words are soma (body), psyche (soul, life, or self), and pneuma (spirit, breath, or divine breath). Trichotomists point to 1 Thessalonians 5:23, which lists spirit, soul, and body, as well as Hebrews 4:12, which speaks of the piercing division of soul and spirit. Their opponents answer that these passages use poetic language about the whole person rather than an analysis of parts.

traditions.view: Many Greek patristic writers used a threefold vocabulary of body, soul, and spirit, though Orthodox theology does not uniformly adopt a strict trichotomy. The spirit is often understood as the Spirit's gift or the higher faculty of the soul.

The Church teaches that the human person is a unity of body and spiritual soul, following Aquinas, and does not affirm a separate spirit as a third substance. Trichotomy is viewed as an unacceptable reading of the human person.

Lutheran and Reformed writers generally hold dichotomy, while some Keswick, Baptist, and Pentecostal writers have held that spirit is a distinct element of human nature. Views vary, and many Protestants treat the question as open.

senses.definition: A short hymn of one stanza, or organized in more complex forms as a series of stanzas.
senses.example: The choir sang a troparion honoring the saint before the Liturgy began.

core.definition: A short liturgical hymn in Eastern Orthodox worship that summarizes the theme of a feast, saint, or season of the church year.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PAIR. Do not stress the final syllable as in Greek; the ending sounds like the American 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a specialized religious term with no negative or positive shift.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly within Orthodox churches, theological writing, or discussions of liturgy. In a Roman Catholic or Protestant setting you would more likely say 'hymn' or 'anthem.' Among Orthodox Christians it is a normal word for the short hymns sung at Vespers, Matins, and the Divine Liturgy.

distinctions.note: A kontakion is a longer hymn of the Byzantine rite, which the troparion has largely replaced in many services.
A hymn is any sung song of praise; a troparion is a specific short liturgical form in Orthodox worship.

examples.everyday: After the service, my Orthodox friend hummed the troparion for the feast day.
examples.professional: The choir will sing the troparion of the feast before the reading of the Gospel.
examples.analytical: The troparion condenses the theological meaning of the feast into a few poetic stanzas, so that the liturgy itself teaches doctrine.

nuance.analogy: A troparion is like a short collect or refrain that sums up a whole feast in a few lines.
nuance.etymology: From Greek tropárion, a diminutive of tropos, meaning 'turn' or 'manner'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable as in Greek, instead of the stress on PAIR.
Using 'troparion' for any hymn; in English conversation, 'hymn' is usually enough outside Orthodox contexts.

senses.definition: In a tropical manner; of the tropics.
In a metaphorical or figurative manner; as a trope.

core.definition: In a way characteristic of the tropics, with tropical heat or humidity; or, less often, in a figurative manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and end with a clear 'lee' sound, not 'lee-ALL-ee'. The -ally ending is reduced to 'lee', so the word has three syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a style or setting rather than expressing feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this adverb in everyday speech. You might find it in a travel description, such as 'the room was decorated tropically, with palms and bright prints'. In ordinary talk, say 'in a tropical way' or 'with a tropical feel' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Tropical' is the adjective used in most sentences, as in 'tropical weather', while 'tropically' is an uncommon adverb.
'Hotly' means with heat or intense emotion; 'tropically' refers to the climate or style of the tropics.

examples.everyday: The resort lobby was decorated tropically, with palm fronds and bright parrot prints.
examples.professional: The menu is tropically inspired, so most of our desserts will feature mango and lime.
examples.analytical: The poem describes the lovers tropically, using heat and lush growth to stand for desire.

nuance.analogy: Like a travel brochure, the adverb paints a scene in bright, humid colors even when you have never been there.
nuance.etymology: Formed from tropical with the adverb suffix -ly, from Old English -lice.
common_mistakes: Using the adverb where the adjective is needed: say 'tropical weather', not 'tropically weather'.
Stressing the last syllable as in 'trah-pik-LEE'; the stress belongs on the first syllable.

senses.definition: With aggression; savagely.

core.definition: In an aggressive, defiant, or combative way, often showing a fierce willingness to fight or argue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The u is pronounced like yoo, which often reduces to yuh in quick speech, and the -ly ending is a clear lee. Do not add an extra dot or pause between the syllables.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes combative or hostile behavior, often in a way that sounds unpleasant or threatening.
nuance.usage_note: Truculently is used in formal writing, journalism, and literary description. Americans would say belligerently, defiantly, or aggressively in everyday speech. It fits well when describing someone who answers rudely in a meeting or argues with hostility in a formal setting.

distinctions.note: Belligerently suggests readiness to start a fight, while truculently emphasizes a sullen, defiant attitude.
Defiantly is neutral about tone and focuses on refusing to obey, while truculently adds a sense of aggressive surliness.

examples.everyday: When I asked him to move his car, he just stared at me truculently and didn't say a word.
examples.professional: The vendor responded truculently to our revised contract, refusing to discuss any changes to the pricing.
examples.analytical: The author describes the nationalist press as responding truculently to every criticism, treating dissent as betrayal.

nuance.analogy: Truculently is like a dog that bares its teeth and growls at everyone who walks by, ready to snap at any moment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin truculentus, fierce or savage, from trux, meaning fierce.
common_mistakes: Saying the u as oo, as in truck-oo-lent, instead of yuh.
Using truculently to mean simply stubborn without any hostility.
Confusing truculent with turbulent, which describes disorder rather than aggression.

senses.definition: Initialism of towed sonar array.
senses.example: The navy's submarine crew deployed the TSA to detect quiet enemy vessels at long range.

senses.definition: Initialism of trypticase soy agar.
senses.example: The lab streaked the bacterial sample onto TSA plates and incubated them overnight at 37 degrees.

core.definition: The Transportation Security Administration, the U.S. federal agency that screens airline passengers and their baggage at airports.

pronunciation.tip: Say the letters T, S, and A separately, with the strongest stress on the final A, which is pronounced 'ay'. Americans do not say it as a word, so avoid 'tee-sah' or 'tsa' as one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. Travelers often associate it with long lines and screening hassles, though the agency itself is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'TSA' constantly when talking about airports, security lines, and travel. You might hear 'the TSA line was long' or 'I have TSA PreCheck'. The two dictionary senses, towed sonar array and trypticase soy agar, are specialist meanings in the navy and microbiology, so in everyday American life the agency is the meaning to learn.

distinctions.note: TSA screens people and bags for domestic and departing flights, while CBP, Customs and Border Protection, handles border entry and immigration inspection.

examples.everyday: The TSA line was so long this morning that I almost missed my flight.
examples.professional: Please confirm your TSA PreCheck status on the travel itinerary before the offsite meeting.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that TSA screening procedures trade privacy for security, and that their effectiveness is difficult to measure.

nuance.analogy: TSA is like a security gate at a stadium: everyone has to pass through, and the process is necessary even when it is slow.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of Transportation Security Administration, created in 2001.
common_mistakes: Saying 'tee-sah' as one word, which Americans do not do.
Confusing TSA with CBP, the agency for border control.

conversation.text: TSA made me throw out my water bottle.
The TSA line moves faster if you have PreCheck.
TSA agents searched my bag because of a jar of honey.

core.definition: To work as a prostitute, providing sexual services for money.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on tricks. The t before r is strongly aspirated and the vowel in tricks is short /ɪ/. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative and stigmatizing; it is crude slang and can be offensive.
nuance.usage_note: This is informal slang found in crime news, street talk, films and music. It sounds crude or judgmental in everyday conversation, so use it only when you must describe a situation. In careful writing, Americans use neutral terms such as prostitution, or sex work when the context calls for it.

distinctions.note: Sex work is a neutral term used by advocates and in academic or policy writing; turn tricks is blunt slang.
Prostitution is the formal legal and academic term; turn tricks is informal and stigmatizing.
A trick usually means a clever act or a magic trick; the sexual sense in turn tricks is a separate, slangy meaning.

examples.everyday: Some people in town gossip that she used to turn tricks, but nobody has any proof.
examples.professional: The outreach team reports that some clients are forced to turn tricks just to afford a room.
examples.analytical: Historians of urban vice show how economic desperation often pushed women to turn tricks.

nuance.etymology: Turn from Old English tyrnan; the sexual slang sense of trick is informal and of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using it in polite or professional speech, where it can sound offensive; choose a neutral term instead.
Confusing the slang sense with the magic or card-trick sense of trick.

senses.definition: Relating to guardianship or protection.
senses.example: When a minor is involved, tutelary powers frequently accompany powers of attorney.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a guardian.
senses.example: My uncle is always happy to discharge his tutelary responsibilities towards me.

senses.definition: Having the qualities of a tutor.
senses.example: Her tutelary manner made the new hires feel welcome and eager to ask questions.

senses.definition: A deity or spirit serving as a guardian or protector of a place, person, culture, etc. a tutelar, a tutelary deity.
senses.example: Each neighborhood in the old city honored its tutelary with a small shrine and fresh flowers.

core.definition: Serving as a guardian or protector, especially of a place, person, or group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOO. The final -ary is pronounced air-ee, and the r is clearly sounded in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests a protective spirit or guardian presence, often with a mythic or literary tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tutelary mainly in literary writing, cultural history, and academic discussions of religion or folklore. It is rare in daily speech. For a spirit or god who protects a city, writers often prefer guardian or protective.

distinctions.note: Protective is an everyday adjective for any guarding behavior. Tutelary suggests a formal guardian role, often a spirit or deity.
Guardian can be a person or a role. Tutelary is an adjective describing the guardian quality or function.

examples.everyday: The old town still honors a tutelary saint who is said to protect the harbor.
examples.professional: The museum guide described the statue as a tutelary figure that watched over the city's archives.
examples.analytical: In many ancient cities, the tutelary deity marked the civic identity of the community and bound its people to a shared sacred protector.

nuance.analogy: A tutelary spirit is like a lighthouse keeper watching over ships from a high place.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tutelaris, relating to protection, from tutela, guardianship.
common_mistakes: Using it as a noun when you mean the adjective in ordinary sentences. Say a tutelary deity, not the tutelary.
Pronouncing the last syllable as tuh-ree and dropping the r.

tutelary.etymology: From Latin *tūtēlārius* (“guardian”), from *tūtēla* (“tutelage, guardianship; dependent, client”) + *-ārius*; analysable as *tutelar* + *ary*.

senses.definition: Capturing the overall sense of a thing.
Characteristically representing something by form, group, idea or type.
Normal, average; to be expected.
Of a lower taxon, containing the type of the higher taxon.
Anything that is typical, normal, or standard.
senses.example: Antipsychotic drugs can be divided into typicals and atypicals.

core.definition: Normal or expected for a particular kind of person, place, or thing; showing the usual characteristics of its type.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the last two syllables are weak, so the ending sounds like 'kul', not 'cal' or 'tee-kal'. Non-native speakers often stress the second syllable or pronounce all three vowels fully.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a pattern without praise or blame. Said with a sigh after a disappointment, 'Typical!' turns sarcastic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use typical constantly for something that fits the usual pattern, as in 'a typical Tuesday' or 'a typical American breakfast'. After a letdown, 'Typical!' means 'Of course this happened again' and can sound annoyed; a natural reply is 'Yeah, figures.' For your own habits, 'usual' sounds more natural than 'typical' ('my usual coffee').

distinctions.note: Usual describes how often something happens for a person or group; typical describes how well something represents its kind.
Characteristic stresses a feature that distinguishes something from others; typical stresses that it is an ordinary example of its category.
Normal implies a standard that is expected to be met, and it can suggest that the opposite is a problem; typical is more descriptive and neutral.

examples.everyday: Sorry we're late, traffic on the freeway was pretty typical for a Monday.
examples.professional: The test set looks typical of production traffic, so I'm comfortable using it for benchmarking.
examples.analytical: A typical member of a category shares its most salient features, though no single instance needs to exhibit all of them.

nuance.analogy: A typical sample is like a slice of bread from the middle of the loaf: it tells you what the whole loaf is like.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin typicus, from Greek typikos, from typos 'impression, mold, type'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ti-PI-kul) or saying 'ty-PIH-cal'.
Using 'typical' as an adverb ('He typical arrives late'); the adverb is 'typically'.

typical.etymology: From Late Latin *typicalis*, from Latin *typicus* (“typical”), from Ancient Greek *τυπικός* (“of or pertaining to a type, conformable, typical”), from *τύπος* (“mark, impression, type”), equivalent to *typic* + *al* and *type* + *ical*.

senses.definition: The act of typifying.
senses.example: Her typification of the three theological schools sorted their doctrines into clear, useful categories.

senses.definition: Something which typifies: which serves as a type.

core.definition: The act of representing something by a type or model, or a thing that serves as a clear example of a type.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on '-KAY', and the ending '-ation' is pronounced 'ay-shun', not 'ay-see-un'. The 'ify' of the verb 'typify' shortens to 'ih-fih' here, so the stress moves away from the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in academic use; in cultural criticism it can imply a reduction to a stereotype.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mostly in academic writing, criticism, theology and philosophy, where it names the act of making something a representative model. In everyday talk, people say 'stereotype' or 'example' instead. In literary or cultural criticism, 'typification' can sound critical, as if a character or group were being reduced to a type.

distinctions.note: A stereotype is a fixed, often unfair image of a group; typification may be neutral or positive, meaning a representative model.
Classification sorts things into categories by criteria; typification says that a particular thing or person represents a type.

examples.everyday: The museum's typification of the 1920s, with a flapper dress and a jazz record, is a bit of a cliché.
examples.professional: Our typification of customer segments is based on purchase frequency, not on demographics.
examples.analytical: Paul's typification of Adam in Romans 5 presupposes a reading of Genesis in which the first man represents humanity as a whole.

nuance.analogy: Typification is like a sample swatch that stands for a whole paint color, showing what the rest will look like.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin typificare, from typus 'type' and facere 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'typification' (the act of representing) with 'typing' (keyboarding).
Using it for everyday categorizing; 'classification' or 'categorization' is more natural in ordinary speech.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, the Greek word typos means 'pattern, mark, or example', and it underlies the theological idea of typification. Romans 5:14 calls Adam a type of the one who was to come, meaning Christ. First Corinthians 10:1-11 presents events in Israel's wilderness journey as examples for the church. Hebrews 8:5 describes the earthly sanctuary as a copy and shadow of heavenly realities.

senses.definition: To howl loudly or prolongedly in lamentation or joy.
To produce a rapid and prolonged series of sharp noises with one's voice.
senses.example: When the match ended, the crowd ululated from the stands, a long piercing wail of joy.

core.definition: To howl or cry out loudly and continuously, often in grief, celebration or a ritual, usually with a high trilling voice.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, UL. The middle syllable is weak, like yuh, and the final syllable rhymes with late. Many learners say it as 'you-lu-late,' but the first vowel is short, like uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to emotional. It describes an intense vocal expression, often of mourning or joy, and is usually used in description rather than everyday talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ululate mostly in writing, news reporting, anthropology or travel description, especially for women's ritual cries in parts of Africa, the Middle East and South Asia. In normal conversation people would say 'wail,' 'howl' or 'let out a cry.' Avoid using it for a simple yell, since it refers to a sustained, trilling sound.

distinctions.note: Wail is a common, general word for a long, sad cry; ululate specifically suggests a high, trilling, repeated vocal sound.
Howl often describes animals or loud expressions of pain or laughter; ululate is more formal and ritual-oriented.

examples.everyday: When the home team scored in the final minute, my aunt started to ululate from the back of the stadium.
examples.professional: The documentary crew recorded the women ululating during the funeral, which the translator explained as a traditional expression of mourning.
examples.analytical: Ethnographers have long read the ululation at weddings and funerals as a socially coded sound that marks emotion as shared by the whole community.

nuance.analogy: To ululate is like a bird singing a long, rising trill that carries across a valley, filling the space with one sustained voice.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ululare 'to howl, shriek', from the imitative root ulu.
common_mistakes: Using ululate for speaking loudly; it refers to a sustained trilling cry, not normal shouting.
Pronouncing the first vowel as a long oo sound; the usual American pronunciation has a short uh sound.

senses.definition: Not ceremonious.
senses.example: The unceremonious way the manager fired him left the whole team stunned.

core.definition: Abrupt, rude or brusque; done without the usual politeness, formality or courtesy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MOH, with a light secondary stress on un-. The middle -er- is a quick, reduced vowel, and the ending -ous is pronounced 'us'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it suggests rudeness or abruptness, though it can be neutral for practical actions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unceremonious for abrupt or rude treatment, such as being dismissed or hurried out, as in 'He got an unceremonious goodbye.' It is more formal than rude, so it reads as polished criticism rather than a strong insult. In casual speech people often say 'abrupt' or 'rude.' A natural follow-up is 'Ouch, that sounds rough.'

distinctions.note: Unceremonial is more neutral, describing a lack of formal ritual; unceremonious adds a sense of abruptness or rudeness.
Abrupt describes suddenness; unceremonious adds that the manner was impolite or lacking courtesy.

examples.everyday: She gave me an unceremonious wave and hung up the phone.
examples.professional: The manager's unceremonious message about the reorganization made the whole team feel uninformed.
examples.analytical: Her unceremonious dismissal from the committee showed how institutional power can erase a colleague's contribution without explanation.

nuance.analogy: Like a door slammed shut without a word: you are out, and no one bothered to be polite about it.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus ceremonious, from ceremony, from Latin caerimonia.
common_mistakes: Using unceremonious for a simply empty or plain event; it usually implies a rude or abrupt manner.
Stressing the first syllable; the main stress falls on MOH.

senses.definition: Without condition, absolutely.

core.definition: Without any conditions, limits or requirements; completely and absolutely.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on DISH, not on the first or last syllable. The -ally ending reduces to 'uh-lee,' and the middle -ion is a quick 'uhn' sound, not 'ee-on.'

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing love, support or surrender, and neutral or formal in legal and business contexts. It is strong, so use it when you mean no conditions at all.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for love, support, promises and agreements, as in 'I love you unconditionally.' In business it often describes an offer or surrender with no strings attached. Casual speakers may say 'no strings attached' or 'no matter what' instead.

distinctions.note: Absolutely emphasizes certainty or intensity; unconditionally emphasizes that no requirements or exceptions are attached.
Completely refers to the extent of something; unconditionally refers to the absence of terms or conditions.

examples.everyday: My mom loves me unconditionally, even when I make dumb decisions.
examples.professional: The vendor agreed to refund the full amount unconditionally, so we did not have to negotiate further.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that the good will is good unconditionally, not because of the results it produces.

nuance.analogy: Like a porch light that stays on for you no matter what time you get home.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) + conditionally, from Latin condicio, 'agreement, stipulation.'
common_mistakes: Using unconditionally to mean 'very' or 'always' without the sense of no conditions.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying un-con-di-TION-al-ly.

senses.definition: To drive or draw from the earth.
senses.example: to unearth a fox or a badger

senses.definition: To dig up.
senses.example: Archaeologists unearthed a clay jar filled with coins beneath the old farmhouse.

senses.definition: To uncover or find; to bring out from concealment.
senses.example: to unearth a secret

core.definition: To dig something out of the ground, or to discover and bring out something that was hidden or concealed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, NERTH. The th is voiceless, as in thin, so do not turn it into a d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means discovery; can suggest suspicion or drama when used about hidden secrets.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unearth for archaeologists finding artifacts, reporters uncovering secrets, or investigators finding evidence. In everyday speech dig up or find out is more common, and for less physical discoveries people often say uncover. Unearth sounds dramatic when used for something minor, so keep it for significant or buried things.

distinctions.note: Uncover is more general and can apply to facts or objects, while unearth suggests something buried or deeply hidden.
Discover is the neutral everyday word for finding something new, with no suggestion of digging or concealment.
Excavate is technical and describes systematic digging, usually by archaeologists, while unearth is broader and more literary.

examples.everyday: My cousin unearthed a box of old family photos in the attic while we were cleaning.
examples.professional: The audit team unearthed duplicate payments that our finance system had never flagged.
examples.analytical: The historian unearths the political motives behind the decision, which the official records had carefully concealed.

nuance.analogy: Unearthing a fact is like pulling up a root: you bring out what was hidden under the surface.
nuance.etymology: From Old English unerthian, meaning to take out of the earth, from un- (out, undo) plus earth.
common_mistakes: Using unearth for something found by chance in everyday talk; find or come across is more natural.
Pronouncing the final -th as a d sound.

senses.definition: Unmatched, superlative, the best ever done, record setting.
senses.example: The dinner was a star-spangled gathering unequaled in history.

core.definition: So good, large, or impressive that nothing else matches it; without equal or match.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, EE, and the second syllable of equal is mostly silent, so say it as KWULD. The American spelling has one l, unlike British unequalled.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as superior to all others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unequaled to praise a record, skill, or achievement, as in a performance with unequaled skill. It sounds a bit more formal than best, so use it in speeches, reviews, and writing rather than casual talk. In everyday conversation, people more often say the best ever or like nothing else.

distinctions.note: Unrivaled means no one competes with it, so it describes a dominant position; unequaled means it has no equal in quality or degree.
Unmatched is more neutral and can refer to a pair or set without a match; unequaled is more emphatic in praise.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's apple pie is unequaled in our whole family.
examples.professional: Her team's uptime record over three years remains unequaled in the company's history.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that the incarnation remains unequaled in its claim that God entered history without ceasing to be God.

nuance.analogy: Like a gold medal with no close second place: the result stands alone at the top.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus equal, from Latin aequalis, meaning level or even.
common_mistakes: Spelling it unequalled, which is the British form; Americans write unequaled.
